passages.title: Where we stood: week 0, two of three done
passages.text:
Week 0, "what to build", picked up where the workshop left it.
56 unique industries in the room. That is the design constraint: "what to build" cannot be taught as a lecture, only learned through exercises.
A hand raise: most had found an observation and run discovery. The plan was still to generate.

passages.title: One sentence from an editor, 2023
passages.text:
About 8 points under target. The CEO and the editors were both right.
The client. A publicly traded media company, the world's third largest newspaper by distribution, tens of thousands of editors. December 2022, a month after ChatGPT.
The brief, fuzzy by design. Walk the floor, find what AI can do, build it, give us a number. Metric: time saved. Threshold: double-digit impact on the P&L.
Eight months. An internal Perplexity on GPT-3.5 for research, and an editing workflow that turned research into an exact 200-word column.
Result: 2%. The CEO said it was not significant. The editors said the sentence above.

passages.title: The room diagnoses it
passages.text:
A patient describes symptoms; the doctor diagnoses. CEOs give incomplete briefs because they are time-poor and vendor-rich.
Wrong metric (Vineet, Shubham). Work that neither saves cost nor raises revenue does not get paid for.
Incomplete problem statement (Purna, Satyaki). True, and normal. Completing it is the skill.
Real stakeholders, bottom-up adoption (Krishnan, Arjit Gupta). Both landed.

passages.title: Killing the four easy answers
passages.text:
Each fix was real. None sat where the failure was.
A better model. SWE-bench Verified went from about 60% to near 100% in a year (Stanford HAI AI Index 2026), yet engineering hiring rose and FDE roles grew about 1,000%. A benchmark measures a task, not a job.
Better prompts. A prompt encodes an instruction. The editors could not state theirs: a good front page is "attention grabbing", "relatable". Ask a marketer of ten years what makes a good hook: "It should stop the scroll." Expertise settles into the subconscious.
More data. Month eight: fine-tune on years of published articles. It performed worse. Full fine-tuning rewrites the weights where old knowledge lived; a new behaviour costs an old one. That is catastrophic forgetting, covered in the fine-tuning lecture.
More time. Time without a standard produces more output at the same standard.

passages.title: What was actually missing
passages.text:
The workflows were fine. Judgment was the bottleneck, and judgment had no written form.
Only the editors knew what a good article looked like, and nobody had written it down. They lacked the vocabulary; the instructor, who had never published one, was the least qualified to write it.
So checking cost as much as writing. A 200 to 500 word article checked for mistakes and facts is, by the end, an article written.
The Verifier's Law: if you cannot write the verifier, you cannot build the system, and you cannot claim the capability.
That is why domain expertise is valuable in 2026: the expert is the only source of the verifier.

passages.title: Same failure at scale: two reports
passages.text:
Capability climbs; enterprise EBIT stays flat.
Source · Finding
McKinsey, The State of AI 2026 (25 Aug 2026, 1,719 respondents) · 80% say AI improved their own productivity. 37% report any positive EBIT contribution, flat on 2025. 6% are high performers (5%+ of EBIT from AI), also flat.
Stanford HAI, AI Index 2026 · SWE-bench Verified about 60% to near 100%. 88% of organisations have adopted AI. US private AI investment $285.9B in 2025. Agent deployment across business functions still in single digits.

passages.title: Follow the money
passages.text:
Five such units in under four months, all paying for engineers inside enterprises.
The 6% who captured value built Claude Code, Cursor, Lovable, Codex. In every case engineers who knew what good code looks like had written it down, so the model could tell right from wrong and the loop ran fast. No secret sauce; a written verifier.
4 May. Anthropic with Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman and Goldman Sachs forms a $1.5B services firm, later named Ode. Goldman: having the model alone does not change how you operate.
11 May. OpenAI launches a deployment company, $4B+ from 19 investors, about 150 FDEs on day one. Its CTO: never a greater gap between what models can do and what enterprises use them for.
April to May. Google Cloud's Thomas Kurian: the era of the pilot is over.
September. Accenture and Google Cloud, up to 1,000 FDEs for Gemini Enterprise. The fifth such unit in under four months.
It is not a technology problem. Most experts have never written down how they judge, so every output routes through them.

passages.title: What a verifier looks like: Ogilvy in 15 criteria
passages.text:
Loop engineering: verifier, threshold, improve, re-score, stop.
A verifier is a written judgment of how you judge something. In 1959 David Ogilvy wrote the Rolls-Royce headline still called the best: At 60 miles an hour the loudest noise in this new Rolls-Royce comes from the electric clock. In 1983 he wrote down every rule behind how he judged copy. That book is why Ogilvy & Mather runs without him.
Compressed into one prompt. For the first 100x website: score the copy out of 100 on 15 Ogilvy-inspired criteria (positioning, unique benefit, headline, reader focus, tone, simple language, evidence, emotion, story and more). A dead expert's judgment, still useful.
Then loop it. Give the verifier, set the threshold, and let the model score, improve and re-score until it gets there. That is an agent; designing the loop is loop engineering.
Do not ask the LLM to write your verifier. It returns the average of every expert, and the same slop anyone gets. Start with the task in your own job where you spend the most time judging.

passages.title: The verify game, round one: an app that adds two numbers
passages.text:
No calculator allowed. Know the process, define the input and output, write the ideal pairs.
The rule of the game: write a criterion you could hand to a stranger or a model so they can verify the thing without you.
Know the process yourself. You cannot verify addition unless you know what it is. Expertise is the precondition.
Define the input (two numbers, not a cat and a dog) and the output (the sum, every time).
Write ideal input-output pairs. That set has a name: the golden dataset. Every ML engineer at the labs has built one.
Input, process, output will be asked in every lecture from here. Most blocked questions are blocked because one of the three is unclear.

passages.title: Round two: has someone cleared the high school exam?
passages.text: Neha's answer, as it went on the board. Another rule-based verifier.

passages.title: Round three: a million-dollar refund
passages.text:
A rule cannot verify this. Judgment can.
The case. Should a Rolls-Royce customer get a refund? About 7.5 crore in India, close to a million dollars. The output is yes or no.
Varun's rule. Inputs: the car's cost X and the cost of issues within warranty Y. If Y exceeds X, refund. Same shape as the exam rule.
The counter. The comparison is trivial; getting the numbers is the work. Shipped as written, the rule can be gamed.
Judgment-based verification. Before the final output, ask a support executive who has done refunds for ten years and answers for mistakes. Same input, different output depending on whether the story smells right.
Judgment has two sources: a human, or an artificial one. Some transfers from human to model once written down, as Ogilvy's did. Some does not.

passages.title: The three boxes: the next eight weeks
passages.text:
Every lecture from here is one box, or the bridge between two.
Verifiable by · System · What we build with
A rule · Deterministic · Python on the code track; a visual builder with Rahul on no-code. Interfaces, APIs, UIs, databases, connected to LLMs.
Judgment · Probabilistic · LLM deep dive. Verifiers as prompts and eval criteria. MCP, RAG, fine-tuning.
Nothing yet · Human in the loop · Agents, artificial and human, and a process for finding which tasks do not transfer.
Ask this every time: how do I verify whether this output is correct? No answer, no build.

passages.title: From the Q&A
passages.text:
Writing code may no longer be the job. Reviewing it is.
Why agents and Python, if a script would do? (Varun) For a fixed process with a fixed verifier, state the rule and let the LLM write the Python. Then: how do you verify the translation? Ambiguity becomes a bug, and unreliable things do not reach production. To verify the code you must read the language. That is the case against vibe coding: if an app costs no effort, a billion people can build it.
Deterministic MVP first? (Neha) Yes. You control everything in a deterministic system. Nobody, the labs included, controls a probabilistic output, only its distribution. One of the busiest teams at OpenAI builds no product and writes evals.
Does no-code skip the logic? (Nishant) No. Combined lectures carry the principles; Rahul's sessions carry the same logic. Code is paying upfront for control, like owning a car instead of renting.

passages.title: From the Q&A
passages.text:
Which tool for a second brain? (Devang) No tool recommendation, on principle. Bring the observation, the North Star and how success is measured; the tool follows.
Already built something? (Jagdeep) Run the exercise on it anyway: observation, hypothesis, what was built. Track switching (Arjit) goes to Rahul at the no-code orientation.

passages.title: What to do next
passages.text:
Finish Assignment 1 step three. Generate the plan and publish your MVP tracker. Due Fri 9 Oct. No observation worth building? Look at what you live now: your job, your peers, this cohort's routine.
Name your high-judgment task. Where you spend the most time judging rather than doing. One line: input, process, output.
Write three golden pairs by hand. Three inputs with outputs you would accept, plus one you would reject and why. No LLM in this step.
Run the stranger test. Hand the pairs and the rule to someone outside your field. If they cannot verify an output without asking you, it is not a verifier yet.
References from the room: McKinsey, The State of AI 2026; Stanford HAI, AI Index 2026; David Ogilvy, Ogilvy on Advertising (1983), read for the principles; OpenCode, an open-source alternative to Claude Code.
Verifier
A written judgment of how you decide an output is good, usable by a stranger or a model without you.
The Verifier's Law

passages.title: What to do next
passages.text:
If you cannot write the verifier, you cannot build the system, and you cannot claim the capability.
Input, process, output
The first principle of building anything.
Golden dataset
Your ideal input-output pairs, written down. Test set for a rule; unit tests for the code.
Rule-based verification
Same input, same output, checkable by anyone who can read the rule.
Judgment-based verification
Writable and handable, but the output may vary for the same input.
Deterministic system
Verifiable by a rule.
Probabilistic system
Output varies for the same input; LLMs. You control the input, never the output.
Human in the loop
Where judgment cannot be articulated, so cannot transfer to a model.
Agent
A model doing a job with tools, in a loop, against a defined success condition.
Loop engineering
Designing that loop: verifier, threshold, improve, re-score, stop.
Catastrophic forgetting
Full fine-tuning overwrites weights holding prior knowledge.
FDE
Forward-deployed engineer: placed inside an enterprise to close the capability-to-value gap.

passages.title: One principle, three kinds of verification
passages.text:
Last week's game, sorted. Everything derives from input, process, output.
A rule. Same input, same output. Build it with what already exists: code and no-code tools. Weeks 1 to 4.
Judgment. No rule, but you can extract the judgment and hand it to a stranger who then judges as well as you. That judgment can now go to an LLM.
Not at all. What Naval calls specific knowledge: what you do better than anyone and cannot pass on. A human stays in the loop, weeks 8 to 12.

passages.title: The summit map: two mountains, four bridges
passages.text:
The four bridges are the only mandatory parts.
The same principle, applied to the cohort, on the 100x roadmap. Base camp is week 0; Assignment 1 is the first bridge.
Stage · What happens there · Bridge out
Deterministic · Orientation, interfaces, your first UI, APIs, database, launch. An end-to-end system deployed by about 17 October. · The hackathon
Probabilistic · Models, tool calling, MCP, retrieval, then fine-tuning and data preparation. · Assignment 2
Agents (locked) · Opens only for those who finish Assignments 1, 2 and the hackathon. About 6 lectures, then 4 weeks of capstone. · Final capstone
From Lecture 3 the tracks split: code in Python with Siddhant, no-code with Rahul. Same destination, different vehicle. Hackathons bring the biggest transformation and the biggest drop-off. Expect both.

passages.title: Round one: a hundred programmers, one machine, no smiley
passages.text:
Two minutes. An old-fashioned machine: no AI, no guessing.
Siddhant became a machine for two minutes. The goal: get him to draw a smiley on his whiteboard. Pasting an emoji or an image did not count.
Input. Instructions only from the Zoom chat.
Execution. One action per message, in the exact order messages arrive. Two people sending different actions: both run, in sequence.
No guessing. An unclear, incorrect or unknown instruction produces nothing.
More than 100 people failed. The room's diagnosis: no coordination, instructions not detailed enough, no one leading. Siddhant added the one nobody offered: no one asked the machine which language it understands.
When a deterministic machine fails, the fault is almost always on our side: an instruction we did not articulate, or a team that did not coordinate. Debugging is mostly finding which.

passages.title: Round two: a common language, still no smiley
passages.text:
Far more specific than round one, and it still failed.
An underspecified command. "Go to 0". The command took X and Y, with 0,0 at a corner Siddhant had chosen. Nobody asked where; someone could have probed with small coordinates until the cursor reached the toolbar.
Commands the machine never had. "Pick a pen" is English. "Circle R" is not a command either: "circle 5" draws a circle of radius 5. Three messages saying "circle" draw three identical circles.
Too many programmers. One machine taking orders from a hundred people does not finish the task.

passages.title: Two systems, and the bridge between them
passages.text:
Language plus protocol. The most important definition for the rest of the cohort.
The game, redrawn as two boxes. Two things were missing between them: a common language, which round two supplied, and a set of rules. The subtle failure: the rules covered only the machine.
The winning version: pick one point of contact. Everyone else sends suggestions to that person, and only they write in the chat. Go to 0,0; nothing happens; adjust; reach the toolbar; click; draw. The agreed rules are a protocol. Language plus protocol opens a channel that runs both ways. That bridge is an interface.
An interface is the boundary, bridge, or point of interaction where two separate systems, components, or entities meet and communicate.

passages.title: The phone call: the wire is not the interface
passages.text:
Every part the room named is still there.
The room answered with parts: phone line, cable, network, signal, speaker, microphone. Fix the language (both speak German) and there are still rules: one says hello, the other replies, each works out why the other called. The hardware is needed. It is part of the interface, not the whole of it.

passages.title: The letter: find the two systems first
passages.text:
The two systems are not in the picture. Name them first.
Answers: envelope, letter, address, stamp, PIN code, even a pigeon. The method: name the two systems before anything else. A letter goes from a sender to a receiver: two people, with pen and paper instead of a phone. Common language: say Hindi. Rules: envelope, address, post office, stamp, fee, wait. Every answer typed in chat is in there, as a component.
The one system doing all of it is the postal service. It sets the rules and runs the delivery. The postal service can be called an interface; the address never can.

passages.title: The meme as an interface
passages.text:
Two images: the I, Robot scene, and the Drake template.
In the I, Robot scene Will Smith asks a robot why it is so often biased and wrong; it answers, because you built and trained me. The Drake template rejects a 50-page document and approves one meme. The answer is meme.
Common language: shared context. You laugh hardest if you have seen the scene.
Rules: the template's fixed panels. Accusation, mirror, realization; or rejection, approval.
Why it spreads. Richard Dawkins coined the word in The Selfish Gene: a unit of culture passed by imitation. It activates context the audience already has, so one image replaces an essay. Siddhant's claim: one of the highest-bandwidth cognitive interfaces ever invented.

passages.title: ChatGPT: the screen is the first interface
passages.text:
Systems, input and output first. Then the interface can be named.
Answers ranged from natural language to "the entire screen". Method first: the two systems are a human and an LLM (software that must run on a machine). Input: the prompt. Output: the reply. Common language: English. Rules: recall the game, where one tool, the Zoom chat, received input and passed it across.
Software calls its customers users (software and drugs are the only two industries that do). The interface between a user and a machine, made of graphics you click, type into and touch, is a graphical user interface, now simply the user interface (UI). In ChatGPT, the whole screen is. This is the first interface.

passages.title: Behind the screen: the Inspect tool
passages.text:
Right click, Inspect, Network, clear, send.
Most people think the screen is all of ChatGPT. It is only the part that talks to you. You do not need to read the Network tab yet. The point: pressing send makes your machine send information on your behalf, at several levels: you to machine, machine to browser, browser to internet provider, and on to ChatGPT.
If you cannot identify the systems behind an existing app, you cannot build one like it.

passages.title: The boxes: where the UI actually sits
passages.text:
Start from the minimum conditions to open ChatGPT at all. That fixes the order.
Box · What it is · Example · Interface into it
1 · The machine · MacBook Pro, iPhone, Android phone, any laptop · The operating system: macOS, iOS, Android
2 · The browser: an application, not the UI · Chrome, Safari, Firefox · Command lines between machine and browser
3 · The UI · ChatGPT's screen · The graphical user interface
4 · The company's machine · OpenAI's machine, serving ChatGPT and the model · Section 12
A user never touches the UI directly. A keystroke becomes an electrical signal; the operating system lets you use the hardware; the machine opens the browser; the browser fetches the app; only then is there a UI. This applies to every app on the internet.

passages.title: The second machine, and the second interface
passages.text:
Two machines that may share nothing.
Typing chatgpt.com starts a trip. Your internet provider confirms a connection, then the name becomes an IP address: numbers, the most precise language machines share. It is the address on the envelope, and it leads to another machine, owned by OpenAI, listening for requests. The full routing: how DNS works.
Siddhant's is a MacBook Pro; OpenAI's might run Linux on NVIDIA hardware. Neither understands the other. The room named the bridge: the API, Application Programming Interface, the machine-to-machine interface.

passages.title: HTML, HTTP, and the rules the room never wrote
passages.text:
Tim Berners-Lee, CERN: a global hypertext system.
Every machine, from laptops to AirPods, shares one language: binary. High-level languages sit on top and map down to it. Before the internet, every machine had its own language, so someone had to agree on a common one.
For the web that was Tim Berners-Lee at CERN. He built HTML (Hypertext Markup Language) as the common language for structuring pages, and HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) as the rules for moving them. Hypertext links to another page; linking every page to every other became the world wide web.
In the Network tab, the first entry after a refresh is a request (URL, method, status code) and a response, originally always an HTML page. One rule is built in: every request stands on its own, so the receiver needs no backstory. That is the protocol the room never wrote: what to send, who sends it, in what form, and how the response is read.

passages.title: One abstraction, many APIs
passages.text:
The kind depends on the environment.
Any two machines communicating need an API. Over the internet it is an HTTP API; you build your first one soon. The definition, applied six times:
Two systems · Common language · Rules · The interface
The room and Siddhant as machine · The round two commands · One action per message, in order; nothing for the humans · The Zoom chat, as UI
Two people on a phone · German · Hello, wait, reply, state the reason · Language, etiquette and hardware together; never the wire alone
Sender and receiver of a letter · Hindi · Envelope, address, stamp, fee, delivery · The postal service
A meme maker and an audience · Shared context · The template's fixed panels · The meme
A human and an LLM · English and about 94 others · Type, click, send, read · The GUI: the whole screen
Your MacBook and OpenAI's machine · Binary, then HTML · HTTP · Web UI and HTTP API

passages.title: From the Q&A
passages.text:
Layers below the UI decide what the UI can do.
Do layers 1 and 2 matter if I only build the UI? (Neha Agrawal) Sometimes not; often yes. For deeper hardware control, they decide what your UI can and cannot do.
Is the common language the interface? (Swasti) No. Establishing it is step one of building one.
Where do binary and Python come in? (Saiteja) Binary is the one language a macOS and a Linux machine are guaranteed to share. Assembly maps a handful of commands to zeros and ones, like the round two list; each language above abstracts further, up to English.
Do I need HTML and CSS for the code track? (Mohit) No. Python throughout, with libraries that translate it into HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The one exception is SQL, in the database lecture.
How do I find 10 people for my manual MVP? (Hardik) Finding them is the exercise. If you cannot find 5 to 10 people for whom the problem is painful, pick a different observation.
My hypothesis keeps changing. Good. If it is not changing, you are not learning. Log each change and its cause; the log is part of a good Assignment 1.

passages.title: What to do next
passages.text:
Replay round two properly. Using only the command list, write the full ordered sequence one point of contact would have sent to draw the smiley. Every message must be a valid command.
Inspect one app you use daily. Inspect, Network, clear, do one action, screenshot. Name three kinds of file that came back.
Draw the boxes for that app. Machine, operating system, browser, UI, the company's machine. Label the interface between each pair; leave a question mark where you do not know yet.
Code track: finish the Big Binary Python exercise. The one prerequisite for Lecture 3.
Keep Assignment 1 moving (due Fri 9 Oct), and log every change to your observation and hypothesis, with what caused it.
Specific knowledge
What you do better than anyone and cannot hand to a stranger as a rule or a judgment.
Common language
A vocabulary both systems understand. Step one of an interface, not the interface.
Protocol
The rules both sides follow: who speaks, in what order, in what form.
Interface

passages.title: What to do next
passages.text:
The boundary, bridge, or point of interaction where two separate systems meet and communicate.
GUI, UI
The interface between a user and a machine, made of graphics you click, type into and touch.
Operating system
The interface that lets a human use a machine's hardware.
IP address
The numeric address of a machine on the internet; the envelope's address for websites.
API
The interface between two machines. HTTP API when the medium is the internet.
HTML
The common language for structuring web pages.
HTTP
The protocol for requests and responses between machines on the web.
Binary
Zeros and ones: the only language every machine shares.
Meme
A unit of culture spread by imitation: shared context plus a template's fixed rules.

passages.title: The room check: who had done week 0
passages.text:
More than 10 hands went up.
The prerequisite was one observation, one hypothesis and one conversation with a real user. Two framing points before any design. You are not married to one observation: until the Assignment 1 deadline (9 October), the more observations you try and people you speak to, the better you get at testing assumptions. And when building becomes a commodity, finding the right users and solving their problem is the part AI cannot yet do.

passages.title: Start from one person, not a persona
passages.text:
Once it works for one person, talk to more people like them.
The observation. Ambitious early career professionals in urban India arrive AI-aware and motivated, but fail at selection, scoping and first proof. They see AI at the category level and cannot turn it into one grounded workflow. It contains no solution: an observation reports what you saw, and stops.
The hypothesis. They are stuck because they lack a method to go from broad AI possibility to one scoped workflow. Test: a workflow diagnosis system plus a guided build sprint, and 60% of active students identify one user, map one repeated workflow, build an AI-assisted version and demo it within 90 days. At 10 people, 6 of 10.
The move. Do not solve for a category. Solve for one named person.

passages.title: The cheapest test is three boxes on a whiteboard
passages.text:
No code written, no system designed.
The hypothesis names two solutions. Take only part one, the diagnosis, and find the cheapest way to test it with Aarav. The input came from a message to him: what is the one thing you repeat every week, in 3 to 4 lines? His reply, compressed, is the input. The output is a plan for automating part of it.
The success test is not whether Aarav likes the plan. It is whether following it saves him time, say 1 hour a week. If it saves nothing, the plan failed. Designing meant understanding what the user needs and the minimum solution that tests it. It does not mean opening Figma.

passages.title: Prateek's observation, and the stranger test
passages.text:
One spec from the chat, marked live.
Prateek's: project knowledge exists, but access depends on personal memory and network, so under deadline people reuse the precedent they remember rather than the best fit.
Observation: too generic. "Organization" does not say finance, healthcare or education, and an organization is not a person. Name the one person who hits this most often, with their designation, and write from their point of view.
Hypothesis: no number. "Noticeably faster" cannot be falsified. Add a measurement and a stop rule, or you keep spending time with no signal for when to pivot.
Input and output: good. Senior experts retrieving a specific fact or project assumption, getting back a concise, source-grounded answer they can check.
The format to post in the code track channel: observation, North Star, hypothesis, user, input, output.

passages.title: Ten golden pairs before one line of code
passages.text:
Gathered by talking to real users. If you cannot, do not move ahead.
One input and one output is an example, not enough to build against. Write at least 10 to 20 pairs: the exact text a real user would type, and the output that would solve their problem. If you are the user, write them yourself and check them with people like you. This is the golden dataset; it returns in the probabilistic module for evals and fine-tuning.
Recall the Lecture 1 game: to verify an app that adds two numbers, you write 1 + 2 = 3 and a few more, and compare. The golden dataset is what tells you whether your verifier will be deterministic, probabilistic or a human in the loop.

passages.title: The verifier is a threshold, worked in minutes
passages.text:
Same plan shape, same tool. One passes, one fails.
Say the email step is Aarav's biggest time sink: 15 minutes a day by hand. With the plan it takes 5. That saves 10 a day, 50 minutes over a 5-day week, close to the 1 hour bar. The plan passes. If the plan only cuts it to 10 minutes, that is 25 minutes a week, and it fails.
A good output clears a number you wrote down before you built anything. Without a threshold it is a demo, not impact.
The written verifier for Aarav's first golden pair asked for four things in the output: a metric with a baseline, the named bottleneck, a test on past input with known answers, and a list of what is out of scope.

passages.title: Test-driven development, written in English
passages.text:
Only the language changes. The philosophy does not.
Test-driven development (TDD) says write the test before the software; once the software passes your codified tests, you know it works. Hard to keep up, so few people do. What changes now is the language: most of your tests will be in English.
Almost everyone uses AI, utilization sits under 20%, and the impact on real earnings is in single digits. Building without a verifier is how that gap stays wide. Mask anything proprietary (percentages, or X, Y, Z) but share the spec, because that is what makes feedback possible.

passages.title: Two systems, one interface
passages.text:
Lecture 2's question, applied to Aarav.
Two systems: Aarav, and a workflow plan generator that can run on a machine. Anupma named what sits between: a user interface, with a common language (English, text fields) and rules (the web's HTTP). Golden pair 1, written live:
"I'm a business analyst at a mid-sized IT company in Pune. Every Friday, I make the weekly status report for our client. I open Jira, filter tickets closed this week, copy them into a Word template, then go through email and Slack to find blockers... Takes around 3 hours. My manager usually edits the risk section because I miss things."
Input type: text. Output type: text. So you can run a manual MVP before building anything: take Aarav's description on a call, write the plan yourself (with or without ChatGPT), send it, and see if it saves him time.

passages.title: The vote that lost
passages.text:
The majority choice fell to one realistic follow-up.
Interface · Votes · What the replay showed
Search box · 17 · No memory, no context. A follow-up means retyping the whole description, and an AI plan may come back different each run.
Form · 3 · Fields Aarav does not need, and no way to ask about the plan once it arrives.
Chat · 13 · Holds context, supports follow-ups until Aarav is satisfied. The winner.
Siddhant replayed the golden output, a day-by-day build plan with time saved as the metric, and Aarav asked: "What does backtesting mean?" How do you ask Google a follow-up? Swasti named the cost: remember the plan, retype, search again. Anupma named the missing property: no memory, no context. Bhavani added that it does not look like a conversation.
Pick the interface after you replay the user's conversation with your ideal output, never before.

passages.title: The vote that lost
passages.text: Rule of thumb: about 90% of first problems fit one of three. One query, one answer: search. Many inputs: form. Follow-ups that need memory: chat. Build the cheapest one first and add nothing until it is verified. That is the V0, or MVP.

passages.title: Vibe code or first principles: the difference is control
passages.text:
Siddhant did not say which is better. Do both.
Vibe code it with one prompt to Claude Code, Lovable, OpenAI or Gemini. Or write it from first principles in Python, AI allowed, understanding what every line does and why. Both produce a working chat. Tonight's task: do both and write a three-line review of what each gave you.

passages.title: Why Python, and why Gradio
passages.text:
Python libraries now bridge the gap to the web.
The web is HTML; styling and scripting grew around it, and Python was never part of it. Until about 2021 Siddhant taught UI in JavaScript, HTML and CSS, and beginners had to learn three languages to ship one thing.
Library · Use it for
Gradio · Chat, forms, search-style inputs: any interface without heavy charts. Siddhant's default. Part of Hugging Face; AUTOMATIC1111, the Stable Diffusion UI with about 165,000 GitHub stars, runs on it.
Streamlit · Data-heavy front ends: dashboards and charts that update. Comes later.

passages.title: Four lines that are the whiteboard
Setting up, and the errors you should want tonight
passages.text:
Solving them yourself starts the debugging muscle.
Install Python from python.org.
Install one IDE: Google Antigravity, Cursor or VS Code. An IDE is a notepad for code where you read and review before you push anything anywhere. VS Code is free; Antigravity is free with generous limits; Cursor has a paid plan for its models.
Make a folder, open it in the IDE, create app.py and paste the Hello World.
Run pip install gradio, then python app.py, and open the local link it prints.
If def, return and functions are unfamiliar, finish the Big Binary Python prerequisite first; lectures will not teach Python syntax. The next office hour reviews your work and your errors, then puts it on a shareable link.

passages.title: From the Q&A
passages.text:
Naming the solution in the first line leaves nothing to decide by.
Trackers in, exception table out: form or chat? (Charu) No answer without the spec. Walk your user's journey the way we walked Aarav's, then ask.
My project is building WhatsApp agents. (Kandarp) That is solution-first. Start from observation, input, output and process.
My hypothesis changes after every interview. Then do not build yet. To learn the process, use Aarav's documents. Spend real build hours only on a problem you can test with real people.
First time coding, from marketing. (Saiteja) You have company: across cohorts the split moved to about 60-40 first-time coders. Siddhant's own start: in a first-year break, one app a day, end to end, on a link, for 30 days. Today's is Hello World.
Not sure my problem is big or monetizable. (Mayuresh) It does not have to be. A Cohort 6 non-coder built 100+ apps in 3 months and has since raised funding. Volume compounds only if the projects point the same way.
Should the North Star be a product? No. It is a direction. Most reduce to a better job (define the role) or building something of your own (define what and for whom), six months out.

Write 10 golden pairs with a real user, plus one verifier with a baseline and a threshold.

Build the chat twice (vibe coded and first principles) and write the three-line review.
All five are in the practice set.
Observation
What you saw a real person struggle with, from lived experience, with no solution in it.
Hypothesis
Your assumed cause plus a test with a number, a deadline and a stop rule.
Designing
Working out what the user needs and the minimum solution that tests it.
Golden dataset
Ideal input and output pairs from real users: 10 to 20 to start, 100 to 200 for production.
Verifier

passages.title: What to do next
passages.text:
The check that decides if an output is good, usually a threshold against a baseline.
TDD
Write the test before the software; now the test is often in English.
Spec
Observation, North Star, hypothesis, user, golden dataset, verifiers.
User interface
The interface between a human and a machine: a common language plus rules.
Manual MVP
Running the input to output loop by hand before building any technology.
V0 / MVP
The cheapest build that can test the hypothesis, and nothing more.
Process
The function that turns input into output.
IDE
An editor for reading, writing and reviewing code on your machine.

passages.title: How These Notes Are Organised
passages.text: Sections 1 to 4 are what we did in the lecture: Round Three, the six parts, and the CRUD quiz. Section 5 is what you do this week: the steps in the Request Builder, then the practice set. Section 6 is an optional deep dive into why the six parts exist, from Morse to JSON.

passages.title: A Face With No Brain
passages.text:
Last week your UI took Aarav's workflow and handed it straight back. Type "I open Jira, read the week's tickets, write a status report and post it on Slack", and it returns the same words. It has a face and no brain.
The brain you want is a model that reads the workflow and writes a plan. That model does not live inside your page. It lives on another machine, owned by someone else. So the question is: how does your UI talk to a machine it has never met?
Input
Process
Output
The arrow in the middle is the second interface. The first was the UI, between a person and a machine. The second is between two machines: the API.

passages.title: Round Three: The Machine That Answers in Codes
passages.text:
In Lecture 2 the machine stayed silent, and every attempt failed without a clue. In Round Three the machine answered every message with a number and at most five words. That one change meant every failure carried information.
The task: Aarav has built a Diagnosis Service. It turns a description of a workflow into a diagnosis. Get a diagnosis of Aarav's Friday report. Instructions only through the Zoom chat, one line per message. The machine does not guess.
Here is what the machine replied, and what each reply forced you to add:
Reply · What had been sent · The part it forced
429 Too many requests. One sender. · Several people typing at once · One point of contact, from Lecture 2
404 Not found. Doors: /aarav/workflows /aarav/diagnoses · No address, or the wrong one · address
400 Which action? CREATE READ UPDATE DELETE · A sentence describing the wish, with no action named · action

passages.title: Round Three: The Machine That Answers in Codes
passages.text:
405 This door takes CREATE, READ · An UPDATE or DELETE sent to the diagnosis door · action
200 [] Nothing to read yet · A READ for a diagnosis that did not exist yet · Read only fetches what already exists
401 Who are you? Key needed · No key · key
401 Key leaked. Revoked. · The key pasted in the public chat · Keys are secrets and travel privately
400 Can't read. Send {"workflow": "..."} · The workflow as a plain sentence · package in an agreed format
201 Created · Everything right, sent by DM · Done: a diagnosis came back
Three of those replies deserve a second look.
Where did the address come from? Nobody was given it. The first message without one came back 404 with a list of doors. The machine itself told you where to knock.

passages.title: Round Three: The Machine That Answers in Codes
passages.text:
The 200 that gave you nothing. Reading the diagnoses before any existed came back 200 with an empty list. The request was understood. It was the wrong request. A 200 means "your request was fine", not "you got what you wanted".
The leaked key. The key was handed out privately, by DM. The winning message had to carry it, so the winning message had to travel privately too. A private channel for the key is exactly what the S in HTTPS gives you on the web.
The winning message, sent by DM:
And the machine replied 201 Created, with the diagnosis: Repeated pattern: a weekly status report. Bottleneck: reading every ticket to find what changed. First AI step: draft the report from a Jira export; Aarav edits and posts it.
Nobody listed these parts before the game. The machine's replies did, one at a time.

passages.title: The Six Parts, Named
passages.text:
After the game, each reply was connected back to a part of the message. Draw the letter from Lecture 2 again: everything on it now has a name.
Part · In the game · Its name on the web
address · /aarav/diagnoses · URL, or endpoint. The domain names the machine; the path (/aarav/diagnoses) names the door
action · CREATE, READ, UPDATE, DELETE · Method: POST, GET, PUT or PATCH, DELETE
key · key: •••• · A header: Authorization: Bearer <key>. "Bearer" means whoever bears this key is let in
package · {"workflow": "..."} · The body, written in JSON
code · 429, 404, 400, 405, 401, 201 · Status code
package back · The diagnosis · The response body
Everything on that envelope together is an HTTP API request. In Lecture 2 you named the API. In this lecture you opened it.

passages.title: The Six Parts, Named
passages.text: The same two principles hold. Input → Process → Output: the request is the input, the machine at the other end is the process, the reply is the output. An interface is a common language plus a protocol: JSON is the common language for the package; HTTP is the protocol for everything around it.

passages.title: The CRUD Quiz: Create, Read, Update, Delete
passages.text:
The game's actions were four words. They are the four things you can do to anything stored: Create, Read, Update, Delete, or CRUD. On the wire, each is spelled as an HTTP method.
Aarav's action · CRUD · Method and address
Opens the page listing his past diagnoses · Read · GET /diagnoses
Submits his Friday workflow for the first time · Create · POST /workflows
Fixes one field: "weekly" becomes "every Friday" · Update · PATCH /workflows/7
His UI resends the whole workflow with the fix · Update · PUT /workflows/7
Removes an old workflow · Delete · DELETE /workflows/7
PUT and PATCH are both Update. PUT replaces the whole thing; PATCH changes part of it.
Google search versus asking an LLM
Search for something on Google and look at the address bar: google.com/search?q=…. That is a GET. Ask ChatGPT the same thing, or call a model through an API, and the request is a POST. Why is one a Read and the other a Create?

passages.title: The CRUD Quiz: Create, Read, Update, Delete
passages.text:
Google is reading. The pages it searches already sit in its index, and your search fetches results from what is already there. Your question fits in the address, and nothing new is stored.
The model is creating. Your message and a new reply are added to the conversation, and that reply did not exist before you asked. Ask the same question twice and you get two different replies. Your prompt also travels as a package in the body, because it can be long and private, and an address is neither. So generation is a Create, and Create is spelled POST.
The rule. Read what already exists: GET, and nothing changes. Create something new: POST. Update it: PUT or PATCH. Delete it: DELETE.
Companies do not always follow the convention. For any app, its real traffic is the truth. You will read real traffic yourself in step 7 of the Request Builder.

passages.title: What You Do This Week
passages.text:
The lecture stopped at the parts. This week you send real requests yourself, in the browser, for both tracks. Do the steps in order; each one has a checkpoint.
Read: your first GET, and the space. The address bar is already an API tool. You will also see why a space becomes %20, and why a raw space causes a 400.
Create: send a package. A POST carries a body. Why does the body need a header that says it is JSON? Because JSON is a format both sides must agree on, and the machine does not guess the format.
Replay Round Three for real. The machine from the game is real. Create a key, then Create a diagnosis, and get the same 201.
Break it on purpose. Cause a 400, 401, 404 and 405 yourself, and note which part each one points to.
Whose fault: every code. The first digit tells you before anything else: 2xx worked, 4xx you sent something wrong, 5xx their machine failed.

passages.title: What You Do This Week
passages.text:
Read real traffic. Open DevTools and find the six parts in requests you just sent, then in ChatGPT's.
Put a model behind it. Send Aarav's workflow to a model on Groq. Send the same request twice. Aarav's service gave the same diagnosis twice; the model will not. The door is deterministic; what comes through it is probabilistic. Which answer is right, and who decides?
Find your key, and where it should live. Your key is visible in DevTools. That is why keys live in a backend, never in a page.
Design your API. Write Aarav's table for your own app, then submit the practice set.

passages.title: Optional Deep Dive: Why These Six Parts?
passages.text: Round Three showed that the parts exist. It did not show why. Each part is there because an earlier system failed in a specific way: a wire that is only on or off (Morse code), machines without a human operator (ASCII), a million machines and lost messages (TCP/IP gave the address), a machine that does not know what you want (HTTP gave the action, the key and the code), fifty companies with fifty verb lists (REST gave nouns and CRUD), and two programs in different languages (JSON gave the package). The Wire lets you work through each problem before you see its answer. It takes about 20 minutes and is not required for the practice set.

passages.title: Words You Met
passages.text:
API
The interface between two machines: a common language plus a protocol.
Request
Address, action, key, package.
Response
Code and package.
URL / endpoint
The address: the machine (domain) and the door (path).
Method
How the action is spelled: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE.
CRUD
Create, Read, Update, Delete: the four actions on anything stored.
Header
A line written on the envelope, read without opening the letter. The key goes here.
Bearer
Whoever bears this key is let in. Written as Authorization: Bearer <key>.
Body
The package inside the envelope.
JSON
A text format, not a language: keys and values in curly braces.
Status code
Three digits on the reply. 2xx worked, 4xx yours, 5xx theirs.
HTTPS
HTTP in a sealed envelope, so nobody on the way can read your key.
REST
A design style: nouns as addresses, CRUD as verbs. Not a protocol.
Backend
The machine between your UI and everything else. It holds keys and stores data.
Four things in, two things out.

passages.title: Where We Left Off: A Chat That Repeats You
passages.text:
The Gradio app from the last code lecture: message is the input, the return line is the output, and there is nothing in between.
What you have to find is the process: the step that turns your user's input into an output they can use. You cannot write the process for a problem you have not done by hand.

passages.title: The Verifier Most People Skipped
passages.text:
A spec has three parts: the person, the golden dataset (ideal input and ideal output, written after talking to real users) and the verifier, a written condition that tells you whether an output is good. If you cannot tell a good output from a bad one in your user's domain, do not build yet.
Adding two numbers, an exam result and a refund decision gave three families: verification by rule, by judgment, and unverifiable. A system that gives the same output for the same input every time is deterministic, and this part of Module 2 lives there.

passages.title: Why Learn It When Agents Can Write It
passages.text: Thinking can be outsourced. Understanding cannot. We are not learning code to write it faster by hand. We are learning how deterministic systems behave, because a system you do not understand is a system you cannot verify: an agent, a mobile app or legacy enterprise software.

passages.title: Filling the Process With One Line
passages.text:
With the manual work for Aarav done, the process fits in one line of pseudocode:
The prompt is the valuable part: the instruction refined after talking to real Aaravs. The task was to make that line real with a Groq key (console.groq.com/keys) and GPT OSS 120B, free at 30 requests per minute.

passages.title: Four Minutes, and What the Machine Said
passages.text:
Deep · An OpenAI client pointed at the Groq address. Errors: missing API key, then gr not defined. Every error is a hint about what broke.
Anand · LLM was never defined, so the call could not run.
Bhavani · It ran: the only working answer of the first three. It also carried things nobody asked for and no prompt at all.
Abhinand · Cleanest: template kept, process filled. But the interface was swapped, names changed for no reason, and the prompt was the docs' default.

passages.title: Working Is Not the Same as Useful
passages.text: Bhavani's code passed; the plan did not. It was full of code, and Aarav is a business analyst who cannot read Python yet. If the most complex technology on Earth does not deliver value to the end user, it was a waste of everyone's time.

passages.title: The Minimum Path
passages.text: Under time pressure with one clear instruction, nobody changes the interface or adds ten parameters. Extra, unrequested structure is the fingerprint of pasting the task into an AI without understanding. Ask first: what is the smallest change that makes this work?

passages.title: Go to the Source, and Read the 404
passages.text:
Go to the official source before any AI. Groq's quickstart (pip install groq, export GROQ_API_KEY, a short script) failed as pasted:
Error 404. The model llama-3.3-70b-versatile does not exist or you do not have access to it.
404 is the client's mistake and means not found. Not found what? The message says: the model. Change the name to GPT OSS and run again. The status code tells you whose fault it is; the message tells you what.

passages.title: Free Is a Design Decision
passages.text: Groq's free tier: 30 requests per minute, roughly 200,000 tokens and 1,000 requests a day. With a per-user quota, that powers a real MVP for one or two users at zero cost.

passages.title: Where Is the URL? Four Principles in the Code
passages.text:
Tested live in httpie.io/app (a browser address bar only sends GET). api.groq.com on its own failed: DNS finds a server, it does not tell the server what you want. The API reference gives the full endpoint:
The whole Groq API, tested without writing code. You can do this in the browser right now.

passages.title: Prompt + Input = Package
passages.text:
The message content became a plain instruction followed by Aarav's real workflow:
"Here is the workflow of an analyst working at an IT company in India. Diagnose and generate a plan to automate this work, or a part of the work." [Aarav's workflow pasted below]
Both share one content field, but the instruction is yours and stays the same; the workflow is his and changes every time. The loop: chat UI captures input, prompt plus input goes to the LLM API, JSON comes back, you extract content, Gradio renders it to Aarav. Judge it against the golden pair, not "looks good".

passages.title: The Cushion: What a Library Hides
passages.text:
In the SDK code that worked, neither the URL nor POST is visible: both are hidden behind abstraction.
A passenger enjoys the comfort of a car. A driver understands its controls and knows what to do when things go wrong.
Comfort without understanding comes at the cost of control.
In software, SDKs, libraries, no-code/vibe-coding tools are like comfortable passenger seats. They make the journey easier by hiding the machinery underneath.
But hidden machinery doesn't disappear.
When something breaks, what you understand determines what you can fix.
To drive software machines, understand its controls: APIs, endpoints, authentication, requests, and responses.
Use abstractions for comfort. Build understanding for control.

passages.title: Ripping Off the Cushion: requests.post
passages.text:
Same as the browser test, now in Python, with every principle visible:
The key comes from your environment. Set it with export GROQ_API_KEY=... in the terminal; it vanishes on restart.
The content is static prompt plus dynamic message. That one line in front of Aarav's text is the P in input, process, output.
If import requests fails, run pip install requests.

passages.title: Reading the Plan as Aarav Would
passages.text: The plan used Aarav's real week: open Jira, read the tickets, write the status, post on Slack. Useful. Then it drifted into architecture, databases and languages: jargon. The verifier produced a prompt change: no jargon, one step at a time, the minimum action needed now. One JQL line on day one, Python on day two, the Jira API by week four.

passages.title: Any Machine, Four Lines
passages.text:
The raw version is provider-agnostic: swap the URL and key for OpenAI's and the same code runs. No new package, no dependence on anyone's SDK.
The four questions for any machine. What is the address? What is the action? Do I need a key, and how do I get it? What package does it expect? Answer those and about four lines connect your app to any machine on the internet.
Practice targets: the public-apis list.

passages.title: From the Q&A
passages.text:
Make my API run a shell script? · Bash and Python speak different languages. You need a common language and rules: an interface problem, the one this module keeps solving. Send your script for a specific answer.
The key showed in the network inspector · Covered when you build your own API. Security comes in levels, chosen by what is at stake: a to-do app and a Fortune 500 company do not need the same lock.
Host my own API locally? · A recorded video is coming. Watch it, then bring the question to office hours.
Feedback · Your best feedback comes from your own Aarav. Queries on Discord, not DMs; Monday and Tuesday are the reply slots.

passages.title: Words You Met
passages.text:
Process
The step that turns input into output: your prompt plus the user's message, sent to an LLM.
Golden dataset
Ideal input and output pairs, written from doing the job by hand.
Verifier
A written condition that says whether an output is good enough for the user.
Deterministic system
Same input, same output, every time. Verifiable by rule.
Endpoint
The full address of one resource, path included. The domain alone is not enough.
DNS
Domain Name System: finds which server a domain points to.
Status code
The machine's verdict: 2xx worked, 4xx your mistake, 5xx theirs.
Abstraction
Hiding detail so you work at a higher level. Comfort that costs understanding.
SDK
A provider's code wrapped around address, action, key and package.
Environment variable
Where keys live, outside your code, so they never reach a screenshot.
Rate limit
Requests allowed per minute or day. Groq free: 30 per minute.
JQL
Jira Query Language, which the plan suggested for pulling Aarav's tickets.
