passages.title: The Whiteboard So Far
passages.text:
Three weeks, one diagram. Aarav types his workflow into the UI on his machine: the first interface. The UI sends it to your server, where the diagnose function lives: the second interface, an API. Your server sends it on to the LLM on Groq's machine, which you do not own. The plan comes back the same way.
That is two API calls, and each needs the same four things: address, action, key, package. Learn the four, not the tool. The same four connect email (Resend: POST /emails with from, to and subject) or data from Instagram and Google Maps (Apify). You never built an LLM. You called a machine that has one.
The missing box: storage. Your server gets one more box to talk to. GroqCloud thinks. Storage remembers. For now, picture it as a file.
See it drawn, scene by scene: the lecture on a whiteboard.

passages.title: Outsource Your Thinking, Not Your Understanding
passages.text:
Anyone can vibe-code this app in a few prompts. The difference shows when it breaks. Groq's docs still list a Llama 3 model that has been retired, so an app built from them gets a 404. Pasting the error back works for a few rounds. Every round you skip understanding adds to a debt, and at some prompt the model can no longer fix what you cannot explain.
The whiteboard is what interviewers, clients and investors ask you to draw: where does each piece live, and why?

passages.title: Where Should Each Piece Live?
passages.text:
Why does the LLM sit outside your server? Because of its size. Anyone can download the model files from Hugging Face, but they need more memory than your server or Aarav's laptop has.
Model · Needs · Where it can live
GPT-OSS-120B, the model behind Aarav's plans · About 65 GB of memory, plus GPUs · Someone else's machine, reached by API
A 7-billion-parameter image model · About 8 to 14 GB of memory · Your own server
A 421-million-parameter model · About 2.5 GB · Even the user's machine
Anything you ship to the user's machine has to fit that machine. This curriculum site has no server at all, because static pages fit everywhere. Size is one deciding factor, and the class added more: network speed (YouTube drops to 360p on a slow connection) and how often something is used (WhatsApp keeps gigabytes of chats on your phone).
Open thread. Write down what you use to decide where a piece lives. We close this thread at the end of the deterministic module, when the same decision is tested with 1 user and with 10.

passages.title: Aarav's App Forgets
passages.text: On Monday Aarav pastes his workflow and gets a plan. On Tuesday he reopens the app and types "I implemented the plan, but hit a problem." The call returns a 200 and the model replies, but it has no idea which plan he means. Every request starts from nothing.

passages.title: Derive It Before You Name It
passages.text:
The rule in class was to solve this without saying "database". The plainest answers were the best. Keep a memory.txt. After every reply, write down who said what, with the date and time. On the next request, send the file along with the prompt, so the model reads yesterday before it answers today.
Real products do the same. Claude's memory, in its settings, is plain text it writes about you. Claude Code remembers a project through one file, CLAUDE.md, with nothing more than read, write and edit. The missing box on the whiteboard is storage: anything that keeps things and gives them back. Today that is a file. Later it is a sheet or a database. Start with the file and move up only when it breaks. Paying for a database to solve a file-sized problem is the expensive kind of wrong.

passages.title: Where Does Storage Live?
passages.text:
The file is tiny, so why not keep it on Aarav's machine? Browsers allow it. Open ChatGPT, then Inspect → Application → Storage: it keeps about 12 MB on your laptop. Clear it and the data is gone, and you are logged out.
That shows two problems. The user can wipe it, and then the app forgets again. Anyone can read it, so nothing private can live there. Your API key is the smallest thing you own and the most sensitive. On the client, anyone can copy it and spend money on your account. One classmate's vibe-coded app sent its key to the browser, and a stranger spent the $10 of credit on it.
So the storage, and the key, live on your server. The server reaches the file through the file system (read, write, edit), and that is an interface too. Size alone does not decide where a piece lives. Privacy and security decide too.

passages.title: The High-Level Design
passages.text:
The whiteboard has a name: the high-level design (HLD). It answers three things for every piece of an app: what it is, whose machine it lives on, and how it talks to the others. Here is Aarav's app, the way we drew it in class, with storage on the server.
Aarav's high-level design: every box, where it lives, and the calls between them. Numbers name the pieces, so you can say "5 calls 6". Dashed zones show whose machine. Arrows are API calls: address, action, key, package.
Read it as one request. Aarav types his workflow into the UI (input). An API call takes it to POST /diagnose on your server. The server adds the key and calls the LLM. The plan comes back the same way (output). Storage (7) is new this week: for now, a file.
Now draw one for your own app: your HLD in the practice set.

passages.title: What Is Worth Storing?
passages.text:
That is the one question for box 7. Not "what can be stored": everything that passes through your server can. "Worth" makes you weigh it. Store too much and you pay for it, or get sued for it. Store too little and the app forgets.
The answer from class: the least you need to carry on next time. To find it, write the questions your app must answer tomorrow, such as "Aarav's last plan" or "every plan this workflow ever got". Whatever those questions need is worth storing. Nothing else is.

passages.title: Three Questions Give the Shape
passages.text:
memory.txt stored one shape: who, what, when. Aarav's app needs more: his conversations, his workflows, and every plan each workflow got. The lab splits "what is worth storing?" into three questions:
What are the things? Can the app create, read, update and delete one on its own, and can there be many? A conversation passes. "9:12 am" fails: it only says when one message was sent, so it is a fact. Each thing gets a table. In the lab it is a block on Aarav's board first, and becomes a table in Level 6.
What does each thing have? The facts you need to recreate one. For a message: who said it, what, and when. Each fact is a column. Tone is a fact on a plan today. If users could save named tones, it would become a thing. What the product does with it decides.

passages.title: Three Questions Give the Shape
passages.text:
How do they connect? Ask two questions, both ways. Can one conversation have many messages? Yes. Can one message sit in many conversations? No. The two answers give the link its shape: one-to-many (most links), many-to-many (both yes: a third table), or one-to-one (both no, and rare: often the two are one table).
This is domain modelling: the smallest description of your user's world that still answers the product's questions.
Practise it: Level 1 for things, Level 2 for facts, Level 3 for links.

passages.title: Keys and Pointers
passages.text:
Every row needs an address that never repeats. Its words cannot be it: two messages can both say "okay". So number the rows. The number goes in a column called id, and that column is the row's key. A link is a column on the many side that holds the other row's id. Why the many side? A cell holds one value. Conversation 7 has many messages, but each message is in one conversation. conversation_id = 7 on a message means "I belong to conversation 7". That column is a pointer (the formal word is foreign key).
When both sides are many, no single cell can hold "many". A workflow uses many tools, and Jira appears in many workflows. A third table, workflow_tools, holds one row per pairing, and facts about the pairing, such as how often, live on that row.
Practise it: Level 3, pair by pair.

passages.title: Two Rules That Save You Later
passages.text:
History is a row, not a cell. A plan saved in a cell gets erased by the next plan. Give each diagnosis its own row with a time on it, the same timestamp idea as memory.txt.
Rows for facts, files for bytes. A screenshot cannot go in a cell. It goes in file storage, and a row keeps its link, its name, and the message it came with.
Practise it: Level 4 for rows or files, and the hospital brief in the Arena for history.

passages.title: Aarav's Model
passages.text:
Eight tables, each one placed by hand in the lab. This is what goes in storage (7):
Table · Columns · Points to
users · id, name · 
conversations · id, user_id, started_at · users
messages · id, conversation_id, role, content, created_at · conversations
attachments · id, message_id, file_url, file_name · messages
workflows · id, user_id, description · users
diagnoses · id, workflow_id, plan, tone, created_at · workflows
tools · id, name · 
workflow_tools · id, workflow_id, tool_id, how_often · workflows, tools
Every noun in your Lecture 4 API addresses is a thing here. POST /workflows creates a row in workflows. The API is how a request reaches a row. The model is done when it answers your questions. Three for Aarav:
His last conversation, every message in order: follow user_id, then conversation_id, then sort by created_at.
Every plan this workflow ever got, oldest first: diagnoses by workflow_id. History exists because a plan is a row.
Which screenshot went with which message: attachments by message_id. The bytes sit behind file_url.
Practise it: Level 5, the boss level: answer these three on the board you built.

passages.title: Next: The Storage Box Gets Real
passages.text:
Lecture 7, Fri 16 Oct. These tables go into Supabase, and a row survives a refresh.
Client side
The user's machine. The user can wipe anything stored there, and anyone can read it.
Server side
A machine you control. Keys and stored data live here.
Storage
Anything that keeps things and gives them back: a file, a sheet, a database.
Timestamp
The date and time saved with each entry, so you know when it was said.
High-level design
The whiteboard: every box, where it lives, and the calls between them.
Domain model
The smallest description of your user's world that still answers the product's questions.
Block
A thing drawn on the board in the lab. It becomes a table.
Thing (entity)
Created, read, updated and deleted on its own, and there can be many. Gets a table.
Fact (attribute)
What you need to recreate one of the thing. Gets a column.
Key (primary key)
The row's address, usually id. Never repeats.
Pointer (foreign key)

passages.title: Next: The Storage Box Gets Real
passages.text:
A column on the many side holding another row's id.
Shape
One-to-many, many-to-many or one-to-one. Found by asking "one A, many B?" and "one B, many A?".
Many side
The side with only one to point at. It holds the pointer.
Third table (join table)
One row per pairing when both sides are many.
File storage
Where bytes live. The row keeps the link.
Decide what is worth storing before you pick where to store it. Draw your HLD, do the lab, then submit the practice set before Thu 15 Oct, 8:30 pm IST.

passages.title: The lecture in one line
passages.text:
Today: the key left Aarav's browser. The function that calls Groq now runs on a rented machine, behind a URL anyone can call, and the key sits in an environment variable there.
Lecture 8, Saturday: the same server gets memory. Things, facts and links from the Modelling Lab become a schema on Supabase, and the whole app goes live end to end.
Then the hackathon. Two days, fresh problem statements, mandatory, graded on the attempt. You do what Lectures 7 and 8 did, with your own idea.
Done for today: http POST https://<your-app>.vercel.app/api/diagnose workflow="…" returns a plan. The key is nowhere a user can see it.
The whiteboard sketches sit inside the sections they belong to. The storage half is Lecture 8 on a whiteboard.

passages.title: Five things before you build
passages.text:
Need · Why
Python, locally · Every step is a Python file you run first on your laptop.
An IDE · Cursor in class. VS Code, PyCharm, anything works.
One LLM desktop app · Free is fine. Pick one, see section 04.
A GitHub account · Where your code lives on the internet, and how you share it for review.
A Vercel account and CLI · The rented machine your API runs on. Free hobby plan.
GitHub in two words. A repository is a project. Commit is saving your progress, like a save file in a game. Push sends your saves to the repository on the internet. You can commit many times, then push once.
Keep the hackathon repo public. A private repo cannot be reviewed. Code is no longer the moat. Your domain expertise is.
You do not have to memorise the commands. Understand commit and push. Let your LLM desktop app run the terminal.

passages.title: Rent the machine
passages.text:
Your laptop is a personal computer. Shut it and the app is gone. Share the link, go viral, and one person's RAM and bandwidth serve ten thousand users. It will fall over.
Your own server is an independent house. A rack from Amazon or a Mac mini works, and some students do it. But you own the locks, the power backup, the water tank and every attack vector on an open port. Maintenance is the real cost.
AWS and friends are the older rentals. Bare machines. Still a lot of setup before you can live there.
Vercel is the Airbnb. Furnished, walk in, pay for what you use. The hobby plan is free. A paid app costs about $20 a month against a machine that would cost near a lakh to buy.
The rule the lecture kept returning to. Where your machine is, how you control it, what it stores, and how it serves an API. Vercel abstracts the first two. You still decide the last two.

passages.title: Pick one LLM desktop app
passages.text:
Tool · Ease · Speed · Note
Codex (in the ChatGPT desktop app) · easiest · heavy on the laptop · Point it at your project folder. $20 plan, free tier exists.
Claude Code, in the terminal · easy · fast, light · Paid. A terminal session is all it needs.
Hermes agent · harder to set up · fast · Runs local and open models. Most configurable. $20 for 200+ cloud models, optional.
OpenCode · terminal only · fastest · For people who already live in a terminal.
What to use it for tonight. Install Git and the GitHub CLI and log in with the account you created. Install the Vercel CLI and log in. Commit and push. Diagnose an error from a screenshot.
Paid models are not required. Everything in this cohort runs on open or local models. Post your hardware in the chat for a local-model recommendation.

passages.title: Step 01 · The leak
passages.text:
Adnan's question from Lecture 5. If the key is in Aarav's browser, Aarav can take it, share it, and spend your credits. Right.
Strip Gradio to what it hides. A text area, a button, a box for the answer, one fetch. That is 01-leak/index.html. Gradio is a cushion over HTML, CSS and JS.
Click Diagnose with no key: 401. Unauthorized. The key is missing. Paste the key into the file and it works, and now every visitor can read it: Inspect, Network, the Authorization header, or just the page source.
Never paste a key on a shared screen. Do it on your own machine. If one leaks, revoke it.
Three machines, three jobs. The client, your server, Groq's server. The whole lecture is deciding which component lives on which machine.

passages.title: Step 01 · The leak
passages.text:
Why you cannot vibe-code this part. An LLM will decide where things live for you, on the assumption of one hobby user. Nothing errors. Someone just quietly spends your money, or your data vanishes. There is now a marketplace of "vibe coding specialists" paid to fix exactly this. Be the specialist.
The leak: the browser calls Groq directly

passages.title: Step 02 · Strip it to the function
passages.text:
Bare metal. Remove every cushion and one function is left: diagnose(workflow) takes text in, returns a plan. Everything else was decoration.
This is what you deploy first. Not the UI. The UI can call your function the way you call Groq, from anywhere, once the function has an address.
Set the key in the terminal. Then run python 02-function/diagnose.py and type a workflow.
Strip it down to the function
It broke live. The first run failed on a retired model name. Anand and Kandarp called it from the chat before the fix. Frontier models wrote this repo and still got it wrong. Diagnosing it is the skill.
The fix shows up as a commit. One save, one diff, the old model name against the new. That is why the code lives on GitHub: a change log of what you got wrong and how it improved.

passages.title: Step 02 · Strip it to the function
passages.text:
Your exercise from class. Strip your Assignment 1 app the same way. In English first: the input, the output, the process in between. Then replace the body of this function and the API it calls. Groq today, a CRM or mail API tomorrow. The file is a template.
If you strip out the UI, what is the one function left?

passages.title: Step 03 · The function behind an API
passages.text:
Dial · Your API
action · POST
address · /api/diagnose, under whatever URL the deploy gives you
package · {"workflow": "…"} in, {"plan": "…"} out
key · none on your API yet. The Groq key stays on your server.
Put the function behind a route, on your server
FastAPI is the shortest path. Four lines: import, app = FastAPI(), a decorator with the action and the address, the function under it. Read the FastAPI tutorial before asking an LLM to write it.
Why /api/ in the address. One folder for every endpoint, separate from static files like the page and images you add later.
Run it: uvicorn api.index:app --reload from inside 03-fastapi. Open /docs: FastAPI lists every route and its input type. Free documentation.
Class exercise. Convert diagnose.py into this API without looking at step 03. Deepti's shipped first.
The two lines you did not expect
from pydantic import BaseModel class WorkflowIn(BaseModel): workflow: str @app.post("/api/diagnose") def diagnose_route(body: WorkflowIn): return {"plan": diagnose(body.workflow)}

passages.title: Step 03 · The function behind an API
passages.text:
Policy versus enforcement. "Wear a helmet on a two-wheeler" is policy. The traffic police on the road is enforcement. Without the police, the rule is a wish.
Your route is a promise to the whole internet. "Send me a workflow and I will send a plan." Someone will send an image, a video, nothing. Deterministic code has no flexibility. It throws.
Pydantic is the traffic police. WorkflowIn says the incoming package must have a workflow and it must be text. Anything else is rejected with an error that names the rule broken. Two lines, a narrow job.
Bigger than APIs. Lecture 1 said an interface is a common language plus rules. HTTP and JSON are the language. This is the first rule you enforce. The same layer sits between an agent and your software tomorrow, because agents are predictive and can be social-engineered. The deterministic side has to check what arrives.
Homework: read about Pydantic beyond type checks.

passages.title: Deploy, and read the status codes
passages.text:
Install and log in: npm i -g vercel, then vercel login, same account as the dashboard.
Open a new terminal inside the step folder. The live demo stalled on this: the command was run from the wrong directory.
Run vercel. New project, a name, accept the FastAPI it detects. Then vercel --prod for the production URL. vercel dev is only a local preview.
Test from httpie.io/app. POST, your URL, body {"workflow": "…"}. The field name must match WorkflowIn exactly.
Add the key on Vercel. Project, Settings, Environment Variables. Name it exactly as the code reads it, GROQ_API_KEY, paste the value, save, redeploy.
What came back · Why · Fix
404 · Wrong address. The deploy URL alone is not the route. · Add /api/diagnose.
500 · Right address, the server itself failed. The key is not on that machine. · Read the Logs tab on the deployment, then add the env var.
401 from Groq · Your server reached Groq without a key. · Same fix: env var, exact name.

passages.title: Deploy, and read the status codes
passages.text:
200 with a plan · Done for today. · Share the URL.
You cannot type on Vercel's machine. No terminal, so no export. The dashboard is the only way in. os.environ in your code looks there.
Never hardcode the key to make the 500 go away. That undoes the whole lecture.
What the room watched happen. An idea, a design of which component lives where, one function, an API around it with validation, a deploy, env vars, a live URL on a rented machine. Five years ago that was five people: UI, backend, API, deployment, ops.

passages.title: Step 04 · Gradio becomes a client (tonight)
passages.text:
One line changes. Gradio posts {"workflow": …} to your URL and shows plan. No key in the file. The key lives on the machine that spends the money.
Run it against the live server:
Gradio becomes a client, with no key
Write down every error you hit. Status code, message, what fixed it. Post them tonight. Lecture 8 opens with the common ones.
The debt left. Gradio runs on your laptop only, and the server forgets every plan the moment it answers. Both are Lecture 8.

passages.title: From the chat
passages.text:
"My output is a Google Sheet." The format is not the content. Send JSON from the API and convert to CSV or XLSX on the user's device. Keep the API layer thin. A phone without a spreadsheet app still gets the data.
"Can I mock the LLM and build only the deterministic part?" Yes. Start from your golden input and output pair, build the deterministic path, then add the LLM as one more API call.
"Localhost URL in the chat." Nobody outside your machine can open it. Send a screenshot.
"Can we have a gap before the hackathon?" No. The gap is never enough. The hackathon is about the attempt, and it shows you the gaps faster than another week of reading.
"Codex slows my laptop." Use Claude Code or Hermes in the terminal instead.
"Where does the project live, laptop, GitHub or Vercel?" All three. Build on the laptop, push to GitHub, GitHub connects to Vercel.

passages.title: Next: Lecture 8, Saturday 6 pm
passages.text:
Storage as a component. A decision framework: inside the server or outside, and when.
The file dies. Plans saved to memory.txt work locally and fail on Vercel. See scenes 6 to 8.
Things, facts and links become a schema on Supabase, and the server remembers. Scenes 9 to 14.
End to end, then a recap of the full trace to follow in the hackathon. Scenes 15 to 20.
Bring: your live URL from step 03 and your Modelling Lab tables.
repository
A project on GitHub. All its files, and every save you made.
commit
A save of your progress with a one-line reason. Local until you push.
push
Send your commits from the laptop to the repository on the internet.
deploy
Put your code on a rented machine with a URL. vercel --prod is the production one.
environment variable
A named value the machine holds outside the code. Where keys live. Set with export on your laptop and in the dashboard on Vercel.
endpoint

passages.title: Next: Lecture 8, Saturday 6 pm
passages.text:
One address on your API, such as /api/diagnose, with one action.
FastAPI
The Python framework that turns a function into an endpoint in four lines, and documents it at /docs.
Pydantic
The data validation library FastAPI uses. The traffic police for everything that arrives.
business logic
The one function that takes the input and makes the output. Everything else is around it.
CLI
Command line interface. The Vercel CLI and the GitHub CLI let your terminal, or your LLM desktop app, talk to those machines.

passages.title: The lecture in one line
passages.text:
Lecture 7 put diagnose behind an API on Vercel. Today that API learns to remember, first in a file, then in a database.
Every whiteboard from the last four weeks connects here. Four dials, things, facts and links, policy and enforcement.
The repository was updated. Same c8-db repo, now with a.env.example and steps 01 to 08. Every step is a folder; the sections below link to theirs.
Drawn version: Lecture 8 on a whiteboard, twenty scenes in the same order.

passages.title: Local first, then production
passages.text:
Two environments, kept apart. Local is everything running on your laptop. Production is the link a real user opens. If Aarav is using the app and you push a change that breaks it, Aarav pays for your test.
Run the API locally. From inside the step folder: uvicorn api.index:app --reload. api.index is the file, app is what gets served, --reload restarts on every save. Install with pip install fastapi uvicorn.
Point Gradio at it. Step 04 is the same requests.post from the API lecture: action, address, package. The address is now http://127.0.0.1:8000/api/diagnose and there is no key in the file.
Go to production by changing one thing: the address. Swap the local URL for your vercel.app URL, stop the local server, and it still answers. Same code, different machine.
Never send a 127.0.0.1 link. It means "this machine". It opens on yours and nobody else's. Anything you submit or share has to be a deployed link.

passages.title: Read the logs on someone else's machine
passages.text:
Locally, the terminal shows every request. On Vercel you have no terminal. Open the project, then the Logs tab.
One request, read live: received in Mumbai, routed to Washington DC, an external call to Groq, 2.77 seconds, status 200.
A 404 or 500 shows up here first. This is where you start when something goes wrong in production.

passages.title: What is worth storing
passages.text:
Start from the Modelling Lab. Users, workflows, messages, conversations, diagnoses, tools. The full picture.
Then store the least that tests the hypothesis. The bet: given a workflow diagnosis, 6 of 10 early-career people map one repeated workflow and build an app. That needs three things: a user, a workflow, a diagnosis. Conversations, profiles and tools can wait.
Facts. A user has a name. A workflow has a description. A diagnosis has a plan. Each gets an id and a created_at.
Why the id. Two users can both be called Mira. A name does not tell them apart, an id does.
User to workflow: one to many. One person writes many workflows. A workflow has exactly one owner.
Workflow to diagnosis: one to one, for now. Under today's rules each message gets one plan. Whether it should allow several is not your call to guess. Run both with your ten users and keep the cheaper one unless users need the other. That answer only comes from discovery.

passages.title: What is worth storing
passages.text:
The link is the user_id on the workflow. Workflow 7 has user_id 1, Aarav is user 1, done. No name matching. The same holds for an LLM or an agent reading your data.
The industry calls this an ER diagram. Entities are things, relationships are links. Knowledge graphs, second brains and LLM wikis all grow from this same first principle.
A user is a thing, not a fact. Facts about Aarav, his role or age, come later and make the prompt personal.

passages.title: Step 05 · memory.txt in four steps
passages.text:
05-memory-txt in the repository
Write it in English before you read the code. Most of the chat got it. The step most people missed was the timestamp.
memory = open("memory.txt").read() # 1. read what is already there plan = diagnose(body.workflow) # 2. same business logic as before line = f"{datetime.now()} | {body.workflow} | {plan}\n" # 3. time, workflow, diagnosis open("memory.txt", "w").write(memory + line) # 4. write it all back
Why read first. "w" replaces the whole file. Keep what was there, then add the new line.
The user is left out on purpose. For one user, workflow and diagnosis are enough to test with Aarav. Add users when it works.
Test locally. Run step 05 with uvicorn, point Gradio at it, send a workflow, open memory.txt. The time, the input and the plan are there. Persistence was four lines.

passages.title: Where a file breaks, and where it does not
passages.text:
Do the math. 100 users, 10 workflows a day, 60 days: 60,000 lines, and you need to know who wrote which, when.
Two writers at once. Jagan and Vineet start the same hackathon at the same minute. Both read, both write, one plan is lost. A race condition.
Every read and write costs memory. A small rented machine runs out, crashes, and returns 500 to everyone, not just the person who caused it.
The rule of thumb. One user, under about ten operations a day, a fixed window: a file is fine. More than one user writing: think database.
Read-only scales on a file. The curriculum app serves 200+ people, soon 2,000, from one file. A personal site peaked above 10,000 readers on files. Nobody writes, so nothing races. Vercel copies static files to servers around the world (a CDN).
Writing is the expensive part. A database is a file system with fifty years of fixes: backups, copies near the user, rolling back a bad write.

passages.title: Postgres, rented from Supabase
passages.text:
SQL-type, because your model maps straight onto it and it is easy to query. The specific one is PostgreSQL: free, open source, and what OpenAI runs on at 800 million users.
Own house or rent. You can host Postgres yourself and run the maintenance. With ten users, rent.
Supabase is to Postgres what Vercel is to servers. It wraps the database in an API, plus auth, storage and vectors. Free up to 50,000 monthly active users and 500 MB. Tested past 100 users with controlled reads and writes.
Sign in at supabase.com. GitHub login is easiest.
New organisation: any name, Personal, Free plan.
New project: a name and a database password you save somewhere. Leave the rest, including the region it picks for you.
Wait for it to come up. That is a rented machine with your database on it.

passages.title: The same four dials
passages.text:
Dial · For your database
address · Project URL, under Settings, Data API
action · GET reads. POST creates. PUT replaces, PATCH updates part. DELETE deletes.
key · Settings, API keys. The secret key, on your server only.
package · The rows you send, and the JSON that comes back
Two keys. The publishable key is safe in a browser only once row level security is on. The secret key can read and write everything. Today you use the secret key, and only on the server.
Four machines now. The user's, yours on Vercel, Groq's, and Supabase's. Each one is there for a reason you can name. Whiteboard, scene 17.

passages.title: From the whiteboard to tables
passages.text:
Modelling Lab · Database
thing · table
fact · column, with a type
link · foreign key (FK)
id · primary key (PK)
create table users (id bigint generated always as identity primary key, name text, created_at timestamptz default now()); create table workflows (id bigint generated always as identity primary key, description text, user_id bigint references users(id), created_at timestamptz default now()); -- diagnoses: plan text, workflow_id bigint references workflows(id)
Two machines need a common language. The API connects Vercel to Supabase. SQL connects Python to Postgres. schema.sql is the JSON schema of the database.
Types are the traffic police again. A name is text. Send a picture into it and the database refuses. SQL types are not Python types.
Two ways to make the tables. Paste schema.sql into the SQL Editor and run it once. Or Table Editor, New table: add each column and its type, then Add foreign key to link it.
Check it. The Schema Visualizer draws your ER diagram back: the same three boxes, the same lines.

passages.title: From the whiteboard to tables
passages.text:
Learn SQL by writing it. The BigBinary SQL course on the LMS runs in the browser, no setup.
Why the lecture stays on the design. The verifier's rule: whatever is easy to verify, AI will do. Code is easy to verify. Deciding what is worth storing, for which user, to test which bet, is not. That part is yours.

passages.title: Steps 07 and 08 · The server remembers
passages.text:
07-supabase-sdk (the SDK and the raw calls) and 08-supabase-api (the server and the page) in the repository.
Keys in.env. Copy.env.example to.env and fill GROQ_API_KEY, SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY. Every step from 05 on reads it.
The raw call. <project-url>/rest/v1/<table>, with the key in the headers. Filters, updates and deletes are the same request with a different action. Read the Supabase API docs once so you know what the SDK is doing.
The cushion. The SDK hides the address and headers:
supabase = create_client(SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_SERVICE_KEY) plan = diagnose(body.workflow) supabase.table("diagnoses").insert({"workflow_id": 1, "plan": plan}).execute() supabase.table("diagnoses").select("*").eq("workflow_id", 1).execute()
Four file lines became one insert. diagnose and the FastAPI route did not change. That is a modular system: swap storage without touching business logic. Tell your LLM this up front or it will tangle them.
JSON comes back because you asked for it. The content matters, not the format. A spreadsheet user can still get JSON converted on their side.
On Vercel, add the same two variables. Settings, Environment Variables, exact names from.env. Redeploy. Only the address changed, so the code is the same.

passages.title: Whose row is this?
passages.text:
Types are enforced by the database already. Who can read which row is not.
Mira joins. If she finds the URL and a key, one select * returns Aarav's workflows too. So would a glitch that gave both of them id 1. So would an attacker who wants to sell your data.
Row level security (RLS) is the policy, written in SQL: you see only the rows where auth.uid() matches the row's owner. Without a policy, anyone who gets a query through gets everything.
It needs login. Supabase's Authentication tab: start with the email provider. Google, Apple and the rest come with third-party costs. Each signed-up user gets a UID in a separate auth table, and RLS checks it.
Advanced for now. Store first, then RLS for logged-in users, then deeper auth. The Supabase RLS guide has the details. Whiteboard, scene 19.

passages.title: From the chat
passages.text:
"Should we do all 50 hours of the SQL course?" Learning is insurance. AI writes code well and fails on the hard cases, and if you do not understand the system you cannot explain the failure to another AI or an expert. Buy as much cover as you want.
"Is RLS about access or about injection?" Both. It limits each user to their rows, and an injected query without a matching UID gets nothing.
"Where is the diagnoses table created?" In schema.sql, run once in the SQL Editor. Or by hand with New table.
"How do I call Supabase without the SDK?" The Data API reference: rest/v1/, the table name, the action, and the body.

passages.title: Next: the hackathon
passages.text:
Dates, problems, check-ins and rules are on the hackathon page.
localhost
127.0.0.1. This machine. A link to it works only on yours.
uvicorn
The server that runs a FastAPI app on your laptop.
ER diagram
Entities and relationships. Things and links, drawn.
primary key
The column that tells every row apart. Usually id.
foreign key
A column that points at another table's primary key. A link.
race condition
Two writers at once, and one write is lost.
PostgreSQL
The free, open-source SQL database Supabase runs.
SDK
A library that wraps an API in functions, like supabase.table().insert().
RLS
Row level security. A policy on which rows each user can read or write.

passages.title: Six weeks on one whiteboard
passages.text:
The module: what to build, then how. Each box is defined by how its output is verified.
UI is the first interface: the screen a person sees and touches. It runs on the client, the browser or device in their hands.
Server holds the business logic. For us, the diagnoser that turns a workflow into an automation plan for Aarav.
API is the second interface: address, action, package, key. Data lives in files, then in a database.
All of that is orange: deterministic, same input, same output.
One box is purple: the LLM, GPT OSS on GroqCloud, called through an API like any other service. ChatGPT has the same ratio: a POST with the prompt, a status code back, and Postgres underneath at over a billion users.
Drawing this for a new problem is the HLD round. A student interviewing at Anthropic was asked to design a web research agent: inputs, outputs, client, server, data, and where the LLM is actually needed. No code.
Six weeks on one board, and one purple box.
The model is the useful part. The orange system around it is what makes it usable.

passages.title: Why the second mountain is steeper
passages.text:
A UI breaks where you can see it. A model answers differently tomorrow, after an update, or for another user, and even its builders cannot fully say why.
Shifting answers are normal, not a sign you broke something.
The most common mistake: reaching for the LLM first, even for jobs it is bad at, like storing information.
Start left of the line. Move a step into the purple box only when you cannot verify its output with rules. Given two equal solutions, the rule-based one wins: reproducible, cheaper, predictable at scale.

passages.title: Input and output of the bare model
passages.text:
Zoom into the purple box.
Same framing as the UI and the API: input, process, output.
The chat said tokens, vectors, embeddings, prompts. Each one got the same request: define it in one line a peer can follow. A term you cannot unpack hides the mechanism. Embeddings are not what you hand the model.
The answer we could check live: open GPT OSS 120B in the Groq playground, type text, get text back. Text in, text out. Some models take images and audio; for our reference model, this is the verified truth, and we build from verified truth.

passages.title: The query that broke it
passages.text:
Which track should I choose in 100x Engineers cohort?
The shape was right. A decision framework, assessment questions, a mapping from answers to tracks, a checklist. Close to what a good mentor would give.
The data was wrong. Front-end, back-end, full-stack, data and ML, DevOps, product, security. None of them exist.
The real choice has two axes. A career track (entrepreneurship or career acceleration, set by your North Star) and an execution path (code or no-code, set by your background).
We fixed the constraint: one answer, no follow-up questions. Under that, an assessment framework is the right template.
Right template, wrong data: hallucination. It is why this model, as is, cannot be the career coach on the 100x website.
Right template, wrong data.

passages.title: Can the orange box fix it?
passages.text:
Satyaki's proposal, tested step by step against the line:
Steps 1 and 2 are orange. Step 3 only works with an LLM, and step 4 inherits it.
The design was not wrong. The procedure is the point. Write the solution as steps, place each step on one side of the line. If any step only works with an LLM, the system is probabilistic whether you meant it or not.
Kandarp, in chat: if you cannot write the verifier, you cannot build the system.
Sampreet: if you do not know what the right answer looks like, find a domain expert before you build.

passages.title: The deterministic answer already existed
passages.text:
One API call, one template.
Define the template: how the assessment works, the tracks that actually exist, and a decision framework (this North Star and this background, choose this).
Fetch the track data from the database that powers the curriculum, not the website. The website updates slowly; the database is current. One API call, one template, the right answer every time.
Cohort 1 did exactly this. No team, no credits: each recurring question got its own decision framework as a plain HTML page. Test it with five real users, as Assignment 1 taught. If they can decide from it, it works.
Steps are a process; anyone can copy them. Knowing which side of the line a problem falls on before you design is intuition. Learnable, not teachable. Run it on 30 problem statements over 30 days and it becomes subconscious.

passages.title: Where rules run out
passages.text:
Where rules run out.
Same student, now on the code track. The question came from a real test of an AI assistant in Cohort 6.
No database holds the answer, no template produces it. It depends on who you are, what you can actually do, the role you want, and the market. Some rule will always be missing.
A 100x mentor can still estimate it, because they have watched many students make the journey and formed a judgment.
Verification by rule: 1 + 2 is always 3. You can use an LLM; you do not need one.
Verification by judgment: whether a customer deserves a refund (from Lecture 1). Grey areas, settled by patterns an experienced support executive learned from past cases. When the check needs judgment, a probabilistic system belongs in the design.
Verification by rule, verification by judgment.

passages.title: Can a machine learn judgment?
passages.text:
Humans form judgment from experience. For a machine, the equivalent is data. The room's answers:
Past data (Anupama and many others). Necessary. Every FAQ ever answered at 100x is not enough on its own.
Data alone breaks down (Varun). Context bloats and models hallucinate more as it grows. Maybe LLMs guide judgment rather than make it.
Decision theory (Prateek). Fuzzy multi-criteria decision-making: gather human judgment through surveys, pairwise comparisons and linguistic scales, then turn it into rules. Works for one category of problem, not all.
A human in the loop (Satyaki). A person checks the machine's judgment against theirs and corrects it over time.
Reward and punishment (Samarth). The right instinct, but you cannot deny a machine a salary. What a reward looks like to a model is open for the coming weeks.
It depends, on two things in a fixed order. Swasti and Mustafa got there first: verification first, data second.
Mountains of data, no way to tell right from wrong: the model cannot learn.
A perfect verifier, no examples: it cannot learn either. A person who knows the rules still needs worked examples to build intuition.
Verifier first, data second.

passages.title: The Verifier's Rule, revisited
passages.text:
From the first lecture: Jason Wei on the asymmetry of verification. It is now the guiding rule for the probabilistic half.
In one line: the ease of training AI on a task is proportional to how verifiable the task is. Every task that is possible to solve and easy to verify will be solved by AI.
The benchmarks show it. Graduate STEM exams and competition maths have a correct answer for every question, and decades of past papers. Models ace them.
So read benchmarks with care. Acing a verifiable test with enough examples shows the rule working, not general intelligence.
If you can verify a task and the data exists or can be collected, a machine can learn it.

passages.title: Aarav's Monday, task by task
passages.text:
Monday: email (urgent tickets, feedback, holidays), then Jira, then Slack and a handful of other apps.
From Jira, the top item: a presentation for upper management on what the company can do next quarter to cut spend and improve the P&L.
An atomic task is specific enough that he can be held accountable for it. "Help my company grow" is not one.
Aarav's Monday, and the exercise grid.
Aarav's task · How it is verified · Verdict
Collect last quarter's data from Databricks and other tools · Rule. Total sales minus Q1 and Q2 must equal the Q3 figure collected. The output matches the expected schema. · Verifiable by rule
Research current pricing trends · Judgment. No rule says what to research or when to stop. But his manager already verifies it at appraisal, and the outcome it serves (cost saved) shows up in the P&L between Q3 and Q4. · Verifiable by judgment and outcome

passages.title: Aarav's Monday, task by task
passages.text:
Generate the presentation · Checked against the data collected and the research conclusions. · Verifiable
All three are verifiable, and they are most of what Aarav is paid for outside meetings.
A task becomes verifiable the moment its outcome is clear. The only time you cannot write a verifier is when you do not know what the task is for. That is why the North Star exercise opened the cohort.

passages.title: Verifiable today, automatable tomorrow
passages.text:
Verifiable is not automated, yet. Some tasks have the data, some not yet. When the data arrives, and labs are working on exactly that, they become automatable.
Not a doomsday lecture. It changes what upskilling means. Ten lectures on neural networks change nothing if your tasks are the ones a lab can verify and buy data for. The useful question is which part of your work is not easily verifiable, and how to spend more time there.
Karpathy's jagged edge. GPT-4 to GPT-5: the skills that jumped (maths, reading, writing, knowledge) are the verifiable ones.
Anthropic's jobs as bundles of tasks, with a nurse. Ordering ward supplies: automated (the list and invoice make it easy to verify). Monitoring patients, discharge instructions, shift plans: augmented. Helping a patient bathe: human. Automated is orange, augmented is purple.
If more than 80% of your week sits in the automated band, use this module to shift it.
Verifiable work waits only on data, and a nurse's job as a bundle of tasks.
Before someone else automates your job, verify it yourself.

passages.title: Data is bigger than you think
passages.text:
A verifier is not automation next quarter. How long a task has left depends on how much data it takes to make a model reliable at it.
For scale: FineWeb, a public web crawl, is 44 TB and 15 trillion tokens (words turned into numbers). Roughly the floor for testing even a small language model. GPT-class and Claude-class models use 10 to 100 times more.
To experiment tonight, use an open-source model, ideally locally, not a hosted proprietary one (the reason comes in a later session). The instructor's go-to: Qwen 3.5 on Ollama. Needs 6 to 7 GB, runs on a 16 GB laptop, works from Claude Code, OpenCode, Hermes or any terminal tool.

passages.title: From the chat, and where this goes
passages.text:
"Can parts of a research task be deterministic, like which accounts to search?" (Abhishek) Yes. Most real tasks are a mix. Start deterministic; move a step to purple only when rules cannot verify it.
The next four weeks: a task from your own job, its verification criteria, its data, then a model built or trained for it (the route depends on the task). Context, harness and behaviour along the way. The finish line is a model evaluated on your own job.
Tomorrow: connecting the model to tools, with tool calling. The weekend build series starts now too.
Deterministic system
Rule-based. The same input always gives the same output. The orange box.
Probabilistic system
Prediction-based. The same input can give different outputs. The purple box.
HLD round
The whiteboard interview: design a system from a problem statement, no code.
Hallucination
A response with the right shape and the wrong data.
System prompt
An instruction only an LLM can act on. Its presence makes a step purple.
Verification by rule

passages.title: From the chat, and where this goes
passages.text:
The output can be checked by writing rules, like 1 + 2 = 3.
Verification by judgment
The check needs experience, like a refund decision or a pricing strategy.
Verifier's Rule
How easy a task is to train AI on is proportional to how verifiable it is.
Atomic task
A unit of work specific enough that you can be held accountable for it.
Jagged edge
AI capability rises unevenly, fastest where outputs are easiest to verify.
Tokens
Words turned into numbers. The unit models are trained and measured in.

passages.title: Before the practice set
passages.text:
Your turn.
All of it is in the practice set. Sections 05, 08 and 10 above are the ones to reread first. Lecture 10 adds one step to the same sheet: test one task.

passages.title: The test query
passages.text:
Which track should I choose in 100x Engineers cohort?
The bare model had never seen the real tracks.
The setup. GPT-OSS 120B in the GroqCloud playground: a bare model, not a chat product, because that is what you build on.
The truth is small. Two career tracks (Entrepreneurship, Career Accelerator) and two execution paths (Code, No Code). The site changed after the model's training cutoff.
Score: 1 out of 10. A confident, well-formatted answer built on facts the model doesn't have is a hallucination. The diagnosis from Lecture 9: the data was missing.

passages.title: More context helps, but doesn't cure it
passages.text:
Same model, same question. Only the context changed, and the score stopped short of 10.
Context given · Score · What was still wrong
None · 1 · Tracks made up.
A short block on the real tracks · 5 · JavaScript and Go for Code (Python is primary, Go isn't taught). Bubble, Webflow, Zapier for No Code (none are taught).
The full C8 curriculum as CSV text · 7 · Still named Zapier, which appears nowhere in the CSV.
Two side notes. The answer's framework changed shape between runs: a system that predicts doesn't retrieve. And a sheet pasted as a table reached the model as an image; it had to be plain text first.
Supplying data to a system that predicts reduces hallucination. It doesn't remove it.

passages.title: Why models hallucinate
passages.text:
Karpathy's framing: the model only dreams. The assistant around it is what lands in the wrong territory.
The room's answers: it isn't trained to say no; output is mandatory, so it fills gaps; it is a prediction engine, not a logic engine.
Andrej Karpathy's framing. Hallucination is all an LLM does; we only call it that when the dream lands somewhere factually wrong. The model has no hallucination problem; the LLM assistant does.
The assistant is the whole system: client, APIs, data stores and a model, as in the ChatGPT we took apart (Lecture 2).
Partly an expectation problem. If you need the correct record every time, build an orange system: client, server, database. When data is missing it returns 404 instead of guessing.

passages.title: Trained never to say no
passages.text:
Fix only the context and the behavior still fills whatever gap remains. That is why the score stopped at 7.
The training data. OpenOrca, an open instruction dataset: a system prompt, a question and an ideal response, the same shape as your practice-set sheet, repeated across about 2.9 million records.
The ratio. In the roughly 30,000 records we scrolled through, fewer than 5% were the model saying it doesn't know. It is trained to predict, not to decline.
Familiar question, unknown entity. It has seen thousands of "which option should I choose" questions, never 100x Engineers. So it builds a plausible framework and fills gaps with whatever was common, which is how old no-code tools got in.
Context is the data that reaches the model inside its context window. The word carries through every lecture from here.
Hallucination = missing context + a trained habit of never saying no.

passages.title: Two fixes that don't work alone
passages.text:
A better prompt. Role and goal wording raise the score, but with full context already given, it didn't remove the hallucination.
Temperature near zero. Temperature controls randomness. At 0 with the full-context prompt, it still hallucinated: a deterministic wrong answer is still wrong. Low temperature plus a system prompt is untested; run it and report back.
Any fix you hear is a hypothesis until your own test says otherwise. Write it as steps and run it.

passages.title: Diagnose with a golden pair
passages.text:
Input, ideal output, actual output. The difference names the cause.
Write the ideal input: the breaking query.
Write the ideal output: the 7-out-of-10 answer with the untaught tools removed. Together they are one golden dataset entry (Lecture 1), the same pairs as in Lecture 9's practice set.
Run the input, put the actual output beside the ideal, and name what caused the difference.
Here the cause was in our own data: the curriculum says the No Code track uses UI builders but never names one. Adding the real set (Lovable, Google AI Studio, Antigravity) closes the gap. Missing context is the most common cause, which raises the next question.

passages.title: Automating the paste: a data source and a bridge
passages.text:
Pasting by hand doesn't scale. Automating it needs a data source and a bridge.
You can't ask every user to paste the curriculum first. Automating it needs two things most first designs skipped:
A data source. A trusted store that actually holds the context: here, the curriculum repository instructors write into. If it isn't in your data source, no model, tool, protocol or fine-tuning can supply it.
A bridge. Instructors keep adding material, so the bridge must stay current with no human in the loop.
The live challenge was to connect the curriculum CSV to GPT-OSS 120B and reach the manual 7 out of 10 with no pasting. Almost nobody finished, and the blocker was the same: not being able to investigate the errors. A rented car with a driver works until it breaks; then only someone who can drive can fix it.
You can outsource your thinking. You cannot outsource your understanding.

passages.title: What the model needs to receive
passages.text:
The 7 out of 10 was produced by hand, so we know exactly what has to arrive.
Three parts in one prompt, the "prompt plus input equals package" from Lecture 5:
The input, as typed.
An instruction: "Here is the 100x curriculum. Whenever someone asks about 100x Engineers, use it."
The data: CSV is already text, so it goes in as is.
On paper that is one chat completions call. But something has to sit between the model and the data source and fetch it. The room's instinct was an API.

passages.title: Why an API alone can't be the bridge
passages.text:
An API needs two machines that agree. Neither side here can.
An API needs two machines that agree on a language and rules (Lecture 2). Neither side here can:
The data source is a file. It can't send a request, answer one, or return a status code.
The model is probabilistic. You can't count on it to hold up its side of a contract every time.
No language or rules were agreed. "Connect it with an API" was habit. Ask first what is being connected and how each side communicates.

passages.title: The common language: JSON
passages.text:
Lecture 2's definition, applied to the model and the data source.
Candidate · Verdict
CSV, plain text, Markdown · File formats, not languages. A CSV can hold English, or even JSON.
Binary · What machines run on, but you can't read or check it. If you can't verify, you can't build.
English · Works for one file, then breaks: it ties you to sources in that language and still needs translating into machine instructions.
JSON · Elected.
Every orange system already speaks JSON, the web's common language, so only the model has to learn it, and GPT-OSS already reads and writes it. If the source moves to a Google Sheet, JSON still reaches it.

passages.title: The server is the bridge
passages.text:
Strip the system you have built for six weeks down to the one box that can act.
Reuse the rules. Client and server, URLs, status codes, and the four methods (POST, GET, PUT or PATCH, DELETE). Every request needs an address, an action, a key and a package (Lecture 4).
Who performs them? Not the file, and not the model. The deterministic system.
Only the server. The database goes (the data already lives in the source), and so does the client (this is machine to machine). The server runs every operation, speaks JSON, reaches anything with an API, and already reaches the LLM. Nothing inside it predicts.

passages.title: Function calling: the reverse call
passages.text:
Steps 2 and 5 run the way calls always have, server to model. Step 3 is the reversal: the model asks the server to act for it.
On 13 June 2023 OpenAI shipped this as function calling, now also called tool calling:
Request. Your app sends the input plus a description of the available functions, in JSON schema.
Decision. The model decides whether it needs a tool and, if so, emits a tool call: JSON naming the function and its arguments.
Execution. Your backend, the execution environment, runs the real query or API call and collects the result.
Response. The backend sends the result back, and the model turns it into an answer.
The only new thing is the direction. Until now your server called the model. Now the model asks the server to make a request for it, and the data lands in the context window. MCP and agent-to-agent communication build on this.
With tool calling, probabilistic asks deterministic to act. When an agent fails, check that handoff first.

passages.title: From the Q&A
passages.text:
Move the decision you can't afford to get wrong to the deterministic side.
Given several tools, does every prompt call all of them? It depends on the instruction. Routing in English ("LLMs, use M2; agents, M3") works most of the time, not every time, and routing is where you want no creativity. Better: keep a keyword list per source, ask the model only to extract the concepts, and let the server search the lists. This is indexing; the RAG lecture picks it up.
So ChatGPT goes UI to server to LLM, and back? Yes, as the network tab showed in Lecture 2.
So before 2023 no LLM could reliably tell the time or the weather? Correct. In 2022 companies built their own servers to bridge that gap, which is what you are building now.
Hallucination
A confident answer that lands in factually wrong territory. For the model, it is the same act as every right answer: prediction.
LLM assistant
The whole system around the model: client, APIs, data, tools.
Context

passages.title: From the Q&A
passages.text:
The data that reaches the model inside its context window.
System prompt
The instruction that tells the model how to behave.
Golden dataset
Ideal input and output pairs from your own experience, used to diagnose, evaluate and later fine-tune.
Temperature
Controls randomness in the output. Lowering it doesn't supply missing context.
Data source
The trusted store that must hold the context before any bridge can help.
Interface
A common language plus a set of rules that lets two systems communicate.
Function calling (tool calling)
The model asks a deterministic server to run a request for it and return the result.
Tool call
The model's JSON naming the function and its arguments.
Execution environment
Your backend: runs the tool call and returns the result.

passages.title: Practice
passages.text:
Lecture 10 adds one step to Practice set 1, and opens Practice set 2. Both use the same sheet:
Pick one task you bucketed Automate or Augment, and write its golden pair before you run anything.
Run it bare, then with context, in the GroqCloud playground. Score both out of 10 and write what was missing beside the row.
Practice set 2: write the eval for that task, on your own, about 45 minutes. Paste it into a new tab of the sheet.
Submit it with the rest of the sheet. Next week we build the reverse call live.

passages.title: Where tools and MCP sit
passages.text:
Today is the top two layers.
An agent is a system, not an LLM with a prompt. The model does the reasoning; memory, tools, orchestration, feedback and security sit around it.
Tools give an agent capabilities. A protocol defines how those capabilities are exposed.
Protocol · Who talks to whom
REST · An app to a service, through fixed endpoints with fixed parameters.
GraphQL · An app to a service, and the app says exactly which data it wants.
MCP · An AI app to tools and data.
A2A · One agent to another agent, to hand over work.

passages.title: From Lecture 10: the model fills gaps
passages.text:
"Which execution track should I choose in 100x?" With no context the model scored 1 out of 10, with a short description 5, with the full curriculum 7. It still named Zapier, which is nowhere in the file. Lecture 10 has the runs.
It predicts the next token. It does not look anything up.
It fills a gap with the likely answer, and does not tell you it did.
Confidence is not proof.
A better prompt and a lower temperature help, and neither adds a fact. At temperature 0 you get the same wrong answer every time.
To find what went wrong, write a golden pair: the ideal input and the ideal output, decided before you run the model. Then compare.
Reducing randomness does not create missing knowledge.

passages.title: Priya's shop: the paste problem
passages.text:
The sheet is right. The way it reaches the model is the problem.
Priya runs Northwind Goods, a home products shop. Everything is in one Google Sheet. Every morning she copies the orders into ChatGPT and asks what is pending and what to restock.
Repetitive. She pastes every single time.
Error-prone. She copies 40 rows. The new order is on row 41.
Stale. She copied at 6:40. An order came at 7:10.
Doesn't scale. Five employees need the same answers, all day.
She needs two things: a trusted source, which she has, and a bridge that fetches from it whenever a question needs it.

passages.title: The sheet and its one rule
passages.text:
Three tabs: Orders, Customers, Products. Six orders: some delivered, three pending, one cancelled.
The rule: revenue counts every order except cancelled ones. Pending counts. Order 1046, a kettle, is cancelled, so it is left out.
Product · Revenue
Kettle · 4,980
Mug set · 3,960
Linen · 3,870
Oak board · 1,890
So the golden pair is ready before any model runs: "Which product generated the highest revenue?" The kettle, 4,980. You can check it in the sheet by hand.

passages.title: What reaches the model
passages.text:
Three things go in. Nothing else exists for the model.
If it doesn't reach the model, the model can't use it. An order the server never fetched does not exist.
Send records, not a screenshot. Text with named fields.
Send only what the question needs. A products question gets product rows, not the whole sheet. Tokens cost money.
Right data is not a right answer. The model can still misread or miscalculate. So you verify.

passages.title: The server is the bridge
passages.text:
The sheet stores. The model predicts. Only the server can be trusted to fetch.
Google Sheets already has an API. Why not connect the model straight to it? The sheet only stores: it knows no questions and no business rules. The model only predicts: you can't trust it to run every request correctly, or hand it your keys. The server stands between.
The API is the door. The server is the guard at the door.
They talk in JSON, because every field has a name and can be checked:
{ "sheet": "Orders", "action": "read", "range": "A1:G100" }
One request through the server, with no model involved:
Receive the JSON request.
Validate it. Right sheet? Allowed action? Valid range? If not, stop with an error.
Select the operation: read, add or update.
Call the Sheets API with the server's own credentials.
Retrieve the rows and give every value its field name.
Return JSON. No summary, no explanation.
Model · Server
Understands the question · Fetches the data

passages.title: The server is the bridge
passages.text:
Decides what it needs · Applies the business rules
Writes the answer in plain English · Does the calculations, checks permissions
Same request, same steps, on Tuesday and on Wednesday. The data may change; the process does not.
Keys stay on the server. Never in the browser, never given to the model.
Cancelling is an update, not a delete. Set the status to cancelled and keep the row.
Move whatever can't afford to be wrong to the deterministic side.

passages.title: Function calling: the model asks
passages.text:
Send, decide, request, execute, return, answer.
Until now the server decided what to fetch. With several tools, who picks the right one for each question? The model does. It reads the question and the list of tools, and instead of an answer it sends back a request:
{ "name": "get_orders", "arguments": { "status": "pending" } }
Send. The app sends the question and the list of tools.
Decide. The model decides whether it needs a tool.
Request. It writes the tool name and the arguments.
Execute. The server validates the request and reads the sheet.
Return. Rows, an empty list, or an error go back to the model.
Answer. "You have three pending orders: 1043, 1045 and 1047."
The request holds no orders. It only says what the model wants.
The model never opens the sheet and never sees the keys.
One question can take several rounds, or several tools. With five tools the model calls only the ones the question needs.
This is the reverse call from Lecture 10: the server used to call the model, and now the model asks the server.

passages.title: The tool schema
passages.text:
How does the model know a tool exists and how to ask for it? From the tool schema, the contract between the model and your server. It has five parts.
{ "name": "get_orders", "description": "Reads orders from the Northwind Goods sheet. Can filter by status or customer.", "parameters": { "type": "object", "properties": { "status": { "type": "string", "enum": ["pending", "delivered", "cancelled"] }, "customer": { "type": "string" } }, "required": [] } }
Part · Says
Name · What to call it. Short and meaningful.
Description · What the tool does. The model picks tools by reading this.
Parameters · The inputs it accepts: status, customer.
Required · Which inputs must be given. Here none, so the model can ask for all orders.
Types · What each input is. Status is text, not a number.
The schema is like a form: it tells the model what to fill in. The server still checks what was filled in before it runs anything.
A good schema helps the model pick the right tool. A good server makes sure the tool is used correctly.

passages.title: When the tool fails
passages.text:
What happened · What the user should hear
400 The model sent a status that doesn't exist · The request was invalid, and why. The server does not quietly fix it.
401 The credentials are wrong or expired · "I couldn't sign in to the sheet." Not "there are no orders".
404 The sheet was renamed or moved · "I couldn't find the sheet."
500 Google Sheets is down · "I couldn't retrieve the data."
Empty result It worked, and nothing is pending · "There are no pending orders." This is an answer, not an error.
An empty result, an error and missing data are three different things. The model must not smooth any of them into a made-up order.
A real error is better than an invented answer.

passages.title: Verify the record, not the sentence
passages.text:
Only the record on the right can show you the sentence on the left is wrong.
A model can write a confident answer when the tool was never called, or when the call failed. So don't check the sentence. Keep an execution record of every tool call and check that.
{ "tool": "get_orders", "arguments": { "status": "pending" }, "result": ["1043", "1045", "1047"], "status": "success" }
Write the expected record first: which tool, which arguments, which result. Then run and compare.
When an answer is wrong, walk the chain. Right tool? Right API call? Right rows? Right final sentence?
Don't verify what the AI says. Verify what the system did.

passages.title: MCP: one standard for every tool
passages.text:
Before, every app builds every connection. After, every app speaks one protocol.
Priya now wants Gmail, Slack and Supabase too. Each has its own way to connect, its own formats and its own errors. A second AI app would rebuild all of them. That is the integration problem.
MCP, the Model Context Protocol, is one standard way for an AI app to find out what a server can do and ask for it. Like USB-C: one port, many devices.
Term · Its job · In the building
API · How the server reaches the sheet · The door
Function calling · How the model asks for an action · Asking for the door to be opened
MCP · How any AI app finds and reaches tools · The standard hallway to every door
MCP does not replace APIs. It is a layer over them. If you write your own MCP server for a database, you still define every action and every table it can touch.

passages.title: MCP: one standard for every tool
passages.text:
MCP does not replace function calling. The model still asks. MCP carries the request.
The value grows with other people's servers. Connect to one someone already built and its tools are yours to use.
None of the three makes the answer correct. You still verify.

passages.title: Host, client, server
passages.text:
The answer travels back along the same chain.
Role · What it is · What it does
Host · The AI app Priya uses: Claude Desktop, Antigravity, or one you built · Holds the model and runs the conversation
Client · A piece inside the host, one per server · Asks the server which tools it has, carries each request, brings back the result
Server · The program next to the data · Offers the tools, validates, calls the Sheets API, returns the rows
"Find all pending orders", end to end:
Priya asks the host. She knows nothing about APIs or MCP.
The model reads the tools the host already discovered and writes get_orders with status pending. That is function calling.
The client carries the request to the Google Sheets MCP server. That is MCP.
The server validates it, calls the Sheets API, and reads six orders. Three are pending.
The three rows travel back through the client to the host.
The model writes the answer.
The MCP server is not the spreadsheet. The MCP client is not the model.

passages.title: Tomorrow: Lecture 12
passages.text:
You connect a Google Sheets MCP server in Antigravity. The order matters.
Connect the Google Sheets MCP server.
Discover the tools it offers. Look at the list; don't assume the names.
Wire one tool into a working flow.
Write the verifier before you run: expected input, expected output, expected execution record.
Run, capture the log, and compare.
Three questions to walk in with:
Question · Answer
An AI has five tools. Does it call all five? · No. It picks the ones the question needs.
Does MCP replace APIs? · No. It standardises how an AI app reaches tools. The tools still use APIs underneath.
Does connecting a tool guarantee a right answer? · No. That is why you verify.
Want to make a tool call yourself before then? The Tool Bench takes about fifteen minutes, with its own notes.
Source of truth
The place the real records live. Here, Priya's Google Sheet.
Deterministic bridge
The server between the model and the data. Same request, same steps, or an error.

passages.title: Tomorrow: Lecture 12
passages.text:
Context window
Everything the model can see while answering: the question, the instruction and the data.
Function calling (tool calling)
The model writes a request for an action. The server runs it.
Tool schema
The description of one tool: name, description, parameters, required fields, types.
Execution record
The log of one tool call: the tool, the arguments, the result and whether it succeeded.
Verifier
The expected record, written before the run, that the real record is compared against.
MCP (Model Context Protocol)
One standard way for AI apps to find and reach tools on any server.
Host, client, server
The AI app; the piece inside it that speaks MCP; the program that offers the tools.
A2A (agent to agent)
A protocol for one agent handing work to another.

passages.title: Step 1: the function
passages.text:
The answer lives in the curriculum sheet, one tab per track. A plain Python function reads one tab and returns each lecture with its tools:
# 1. A plain Python function. It reads one track's tab of the public curriculum sheet. SHEET = "https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1Kg6T-dJWaYx_JCPiRk3u0nBuAQcsCVRDPj1NFKP4WzM/gviz/tq?tqx=out:csv&gid=" TABS = {"code": "368290478", "no-code": "0"} def get_lectures(track): rows = csv.reader(io.StringIO(requests.get(SHEET + TABS[track]).text)) return [row[1] + ": " + row[3] for row in rows if row[1][:1].isdigit()]
No model yet. Same track in, same list out, every time.

passages.title: Step 1: the card
passages.text:
The model can't see your function. It reads a card that describes it: a name, what it does, and what to pass in. The request to Groq is the one from Lecture 5 with one new field, tools.
# 2. A card that tells the model this function exists. card = {"type": "function", "function": { "name": "get_lectures", "description": "Lists every lecture of one 100xEngineers Cohort 8 track, with the tools it uses.", "parameters": {"type": "object", "properties": {"track": {"type": "string", "enum": ["code", "no-code"]}}, "required": ["track"]}, }} def ask_groq(messages): r = requests.post("https://api.groq.com/openai/v1/chat/completions", headers={"Authorization": "Bearer " + os.environ["GROQ_API_KEY"]}, json={"model": "openai/gpt-oss-120b", "messages": messages, "tools": [card]}) r.raise_for_status() # 429 means wait a minute and run again return r.json()["choices"][0]["message"]

passages.title: Step 1: the tool call
passages.text:
The same six arrows as the Tool Bench. This time your code is the server.
Send the question with the card. The model does not answer: it replies with a tool call, the name of your function and what to pass in. Your code runs the function and sends the result back. While the model keeps asking, the loop keeps running. When it stops asking, that reply is the answer.

passages.title: Step 1: the tool call
passages.text:
# 3. Ask. The model does not answer: it asks for the function. messages = [ {"role": "system", "content": "For any question about the course, call get_lectures first. Answer in three sentences."}, {"role": "user", "content": "Which track should I choose in the 100xEngineers cohort?"}, ] reply = ask_groq(messages) # 4. While the model asks for the function, your code runs it and hands the result back. while reply.get("tool_calls"): messages.append(reply) for call in reply["tool_calls"]: args = json.loads(call["function"]["arguments"]) print("The model asked for: get_lectures", args) result = get_lectures(**args) messages.append({"role": "tool", "tool_call_id": call["id"], "content": json.dumps(result)}) reply = ask_groq(messages) # 5. No more requests: this is the answer, written from the sheet. print("\n" + reply["content"])
$ python tool_call.py The model asked for: get_lectures {'track': 'code'} The model asked for: get_lectures {'track': 'no-code'} Both tracks cover the same AI fundamentals and product-building milestones, but the code track teaches implementation with Python, FastAPI, Gradio/Streamlit, Supabase and Groq, while the no-code track uses visual tools like Google Stitch, AI Studio, Antigravity and Vercel for the same outcomes. …

passages.title: Step 1: the tool call
passages.text:
The model never touched the sheet. It wrote a request. Your code did the work.
It asked twice, once per track, on its own.
Every tool it names is in the sheet, because it copied them from the result.
That is a tool call: the model asks, your code acts.

passages.title: Step 2: the MCP server
passages.text:
Put the function at an address once. Every app needs only the address.
Your function lives inside tool_call.py. Another app can't use it there. An MCP server puts it at an address any app can reach. This is the whole file:
import csv, io import requests from fastmcp import FastMCP SHEET = "https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1Kg6T-dJWaYx_JCPiRk3u0nBuAQcsCVRDPj1NFKP4WzM/gviz/tq?tqx=out:csv&gid=" TABS = {"code": "368290478", "no-code": "0"} mcp = FastMCP("100x curriculum") # The same function as step 1. The decorator writes the card for you, # from the name, the docstring and the type hint. @mcp.tool def get_lectures(track: str) -> list[str]: """Lists every lecture of one 100xEngineers Cohort 8 track, with the tools it uses. track is 'code' or 'no-code'.""" rows = csv.reader(io.StringIO(requests.get(SHEET + TABS[track]).text)) return [row[1] + ": " + row[3] for row in rows if row[1][:1].isdigit()] # Any MCP client can now reach it at http://localhost:8000/mcp mcp.run(transport="http", port=8000)
The function is the same as step 1.
The card is gone. @mcp.tool writes it for you, from the function's name, its docstring and its type hint.

passages.title: Step 2: the MCP server
passages.text:
The Groq code is gone too. The server only runs the function. The app that connects brings the model.
Run it, leave it running, and in a second terminal ask the server what it offers, then call the tool:
$ python mcp_server.py # terminal 1 $ fastmcp list http://localhost:8000/mcp # terminal 2 Tools (1) get_lectures(track: str) -> dict Lists every lecture of one 100xEngineers Cohort 8 track, with the tools it uses. track is 'code' or 'no-code'. $ fastmcp call http://localhost:8000/mcp get_lectures track=no-code { "result": [ "1. Orientation and State of AI 2026: None", "2. What is an interface; UI as the first interface: None", "3. PRD to UI design to frontend app: Google Stitch, Google AI Studio", … ] }
Command · Asks the server
fastmcp list · What can you do? The card comes back.
fastmcp call · Run this one, with these arguments. The result comes back.
MCP changes where the function lives. It does not change the function.

In Practice set 1, step 04 you tested one row and wrote what the model was missing. That missing thing is your first tool. Practice set 3 walks you through both steps for your own row.
Tool
A function your code runs when the model asks for it.
Card
The description of a tool that the model reads: its name, what it does, and what to pass in.
Tool call
The model's reply naming a tool and what to pass in. A request, not an action.
MCP server
Tools at an address, so any app can list them and call them.
FastMCP
The Python library that turns a function into an MCP server.
